title: Three failed web logins permanently disable EVERY web user account (status=0 written to all WEBUSERS entries; nothing ever writes status back to 1)
detail:
In Barracuda, `updateLoginFailureCount` (0x1537c) is called from `LoginTrackerIntf_LoginFailed_func` (0x13a24) on every failed web login. It loads /opt/tuxedo/configuration/webuseraccountsenc.json, finds the entry whose `userName` matches, and increments `accLockedCount` (0x15538: `add r1, r6, #1`), where r6 is the PRE-increment count (initialised to 0 at 0x154c4 `mov r6, sl`).

It then guards a second loop with `cmp r6,#1 / ble 0x15634` (0x15588-0x15590) — i.e. the loop runs from the 3rd failure onward. That loop (0x15594-0x1562c) walks all five WEBUSERS array slots and, for each JSON object entry:
  - 0x155cc `cmp r0,#3` / `bne 0x155fc` — only if THAT entry's accLockedCount == 3 does it set `accountLocked = 1`;
  - 0x155fc-0x15620 — then UNCONDITIONALLY (reached both by fall-through and by the `bne`) it does json_pop_back(entry,"status"), json_delete, json_new_i("status", 0), json_push_back.
Raw bytes verified at 0x155cc `030050e3`, 0x155d8 `0700001a` (bne), 0x1560c `0010a0e3` (mov r1,#0). So `status` is set to 0 on every account, not just the one that failed. The result is then AES-encrypted, written to /tmp/webuseraccountsenc.json and installed over the real file via validateCRCFileOnFileWrite (0x1563c-0x156b8) — it is persistent across reboot.

`readUserNamePasswordFromJSON` (0x14c??-0x14e??, the ONLY caller is MyUserDB_getPwd at 0x14f4c) skips any entry whose `status` != 1: 0x14dc8 json_get(entry,"status") -> json_as_string -> atoi -> 0x14ddc `cmp r0,#1` / 0x14dec `bne 0x14e78` (skip). So a status=0 account supplies no credential and can never authenticate.

The recovery path is asymmetric. `resetLoginFailureCount1` (0x136d4), whose only callers are authPage_service (0x14290, 0x14434), rewrites `accLockedCount` (0x13884), `accLockedTime` (0x138ac) and `accountLocked` (0x138d4) — and never touches `status`. A whole-binary scan for references to the "status" key string (0x8d768) in Barracuda returns exactly five sites: readUserNamePasswordFromJSON (read), updateLoginFailureCount (write 0), WnmpDir_serviceField, checkTotalUserAccount (read, 0x2c584) and Invalid_html076EF::service (read, 0x387d8). No function in Barracuda writes status=1.
impact: After three consecutive bad passwords on any one web account, every web user account in the panel is marked disabled and the whole web/remote interface becomes un-loginable. Because the reset path never restores `status`, a successful login can never happen again to clear it, and the state is written back to flash so a reboot does not help. The owner is locked out of the web UI of his own panel by three typos, and the only plausible repair is re-creating the web accounts from the local touchscreen (or editing the encrypted JSON off-box).
evidence: Barracuda 0x15588-0x1562c (updateLoginFailureCount second loop; raw bytes dumped), 0x155fc-0x15620 (unconditional status=0), 0x154c4 (r6 init 0), 0x15588 (`cmp r6,#1 / ble`); 0x14dc8-0x14dec (readUserNamePasswordFromJSON status!=1 skip); 0x14f4c (MyUserDB_getPwd -> readUserNamePasswordFromJSON, sole caller); 0x136d4/0x13884/0x138ac/0x138d4 (resetLoginFailureCount1 restores three fields, not status); whole-image reference scan for the "status" literal at 0x8d768 (5 sites, one writer, value 0). refutation_attempted: (1) I first assumed the status=0 write was inside the `accLockedCount==3` branch; re-dumping raw instruction bytes at 0x155cc-0x15620 shows the `bne 0x155fc` jumps INTO the status block, so it executes on every iteration regardless of that entry's count. (2) I looked for a time-based auto-unlock: `accLockedTime` is written by update/reset but a full reference scan shows no reader anywhere, so there is no expiry. (3) I checked whether `status` might mean something other than 'account enabled' — readUserNamePasswordFromJSON's filter chain (u8UserId>0, status==1, then load userName/passWord) makes it an enable flag. (4) I looked for another writer: `resetLoginFailureCount` (no trailing 1) exists but has ZERO callers in the BL xref map, and even it does not write status. (5) I checked the outer guard so as not to overstate the trigger — it is the 3rd failure on one account, not the 1st. What I could NOT determine: whether the tuxedo local UI rewrites this JSON with status=1 when the owner edits a web user from the touchscreen — I could not find a reference to the "WEBUSERS"/"accountLocked" literals from tuxedo code, so the local-UI repair path is unverified.
fixable_how: No client-side workaround. Recovery is a config change: decrypt /opt/tuxedo/configuration/webuseraccountsenc.json and set "status":1 / "accLockedCount":0 / "accountLocked":0 for the accounts, re-encrypt, and fix the CRC sidecar webuseraccountsenc_sec.json — or re-create the web users from the local touchscreen if that path rewrites status. A proper fix needs a firmware patch: restrict the status=0 write to the matched account and make resetLoginFailureCount1 restore status=1.

title: consoleMode is a one-way counter: after the first visit to the web keypad page, Barracuda silently drops the BACK (502) and HOME (503) commands forever
detail:
Barracuda keeps a plain global `consoleMode` (0x55b7d8) with three accessors and no other references anywhere in the image: `setConsoleModeAdd` (0x2aad4, ++), `setConsoleModeSub` (0x2aaec, -- clamped at 0), `getConsoleMode` (0x2ab08).

In handlerequest_html076EF::service the command dispatch is a compare chain. Resolving the literals: 0x3a698 loads 1125 -> 0x3d24c `bl setConsoleModeAdd`; the adjacent 0x3d254 `bl setConsoleModeSub` is cmd 1126. 0x3a758 loads 501, then `add r3,r3,#1` (=502) and 0x3a770 branches to 0x3b3ac; 0x3a728 loads 503 and 0x3a730 branches to 0x3b3ec. Both 0x3b3ac and 0x3b3ec begin with `bl getConsoleMode / cmp r0,#0 / bne 0x3e63c` — i.e. while consoleMode != 0 the command is dropped without being forwarded to the panel and without any error to the browser.

On the web-app side, `disableBackBtn()` in webapp/script/consoleRequest.js line 156 sends CONSOLEMODESTATUSADD (1125) every time the console keypad page loads (eventHandler.js:816 and :847 call `window.parent.disableBackBtn()` when pageName contains "consolekeypad.html"). The only sender of CONSOLEMODESTATUSSUB (1126) is `goBack(pageIDNo)` in eventHandler.js:912, and only when `pageIDNo == 1`. A grep of the whole extracted web app for `goBack` finds exactly three live call sites (newscripts/bookmarksView.js:57, newscripts/cameraview.js:57, pListScript.js:264) and all three call `goBack()` with NO argument; the single `goBack(1)` in consoleRequest.js:111 is inside a commented-out `onunload` handler. So 1126 is never sent by the shipped UI at all, and consoleMode only ever increases.
impact: The first time the owner opens the web keypad (consolekeypad.html), consoleMode goes to 1 and stays there. From that point the Back and Home buttons in the web UI are dead — the browser fires the request, gets a normal response, and nothing happens on the panel. It does not recover on logout or session expiry (no session-cleanup path calls setConsoleModeSub); only restarting Barracuda / rebooting the panel clears it, and the next keypad visit re-arms it.
evidence: Barracuda 0x2aad4 / 0x2aaec / 0x2ab08 (the three accessors); whole-image scan for the global at 0x55b7d8 returns only those three functions; 0x3b3ac and 0x3b3ec (`bl getConsoleMode / cmp r0,#0 / bne 0x3e63c` gate); literal resolution at 0x3b2a8=1125, 0x3b2ac=503, 0x3b2b0=501(+1=502); 0x3d24c/0x3d254 (Add/Sub dispatch). Web app: C:\Users\dev\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\D--PersonalProjects-iot-protocol-tools\000ba43d-52f5-43a6-902d-6c0edfdf3ceb\scratchpad\webapp\script\consoleRequest.js line 156 (ADD) and line 111 (commented-out goBack(1)); webapp/script/eventHandler.js lines 906-912 (SUB only when pageIDNo==1) and 816/847 (disableBackBtn on consolekeypad.html).
refutation_attempted: (1) I assumed at first that the normal Back press would decrement then send BACK, making the bug self-healing; a loose `grep -rn goBack webapp/` shows every live caller passes no argument, so `pageIDNo == 1` is never true and 1126 is never sent — the counter is strictly monotonic. (2) I checked whether another code path decrements on session expiry or client unregister: setConsoleModeSub has exactly two BL callers, both the cmd-1126 arm of the two handlerequest servlets. (3) I checked the mobile app (webapp/script/mobile/script/security_1.js:256) — its SUB send is inside a /* */ comment too. (4) I verified the gated commands really are 502/503 by decoding the literal pool words rather than guessing from the compare chain. (5) I considered that consoleMode might gate something harmless; both gated arms are the ones that forward a 0x194-byte command struct to the panel via mq_send6280App, so the command genuinely does not reach the panel.
fixable_how: Client-side workaround: issue GET /handlerequest.html?cmd=1126&Type=1126&... (a valid session) once per keypad visit, or after opening the keypad page, to drive the counter back to 0. A one-line web-app fix is to restore the commented-out onunload goBack(1) in consoleRequest.js, or to change the live goBack() call sites to pass the page id. A firmware patch would be needed to make the counter self-clearing on session teardown.

title: osal_MqSend discards the ENTIRE queue backlog when the queue is full instead of blocking or dropping one message
detail:
`osal_MqSend(int,char*,int)` at 0x5a78e0 reads the queue attributes, compares mq_curmsgs ([fp-0x30]) against mq_maxmsg ([fp-0x38]) at 0x5a7920, and when they are equal calls `osal_MqFlush(mqdes)` (0x5a7934) before doing the mq_send. `osal_MqFlush` at 0x5a7694 loops i=0..mq_maxmsg-1 calling the timed receive with a 100 ms deadline and memset-ing the buffer (0x5a76e8-0x5a7720) — it drains and throws away every queued message; there is no break on error, so if the queue drains early the remaining iterations each burn up to 100 ms. `osal_MqSendPriority` (0x5a7818) has the identical flush-on-full path at 0x5a786c.

This is the send primitive for the panel's main IPC fabric. `osal_MqSend(int,char*,int)` has 246 call sites in tuxedo, including RequestPartitionStatus (0x585c6c), HandlePartitionStatus (0x589118), HandleZoneDescription, HandleTotalZones, HandleArmingModesResponse, GetUserInformation, sendMailToUser and every CReceiverThread web-response path. The queue those web paths use, `/Q_ServCmdTrsmtr` (mpl_msqIdSendToServer), is created in CReceiverThread's constructor at 0x141764-0x141774 with msgsize 0x22c (556) and maxmsg 0x20 (32); its peer `/Q_ServCmdRcver` is msgsize 0x194, maxmsg 32.
impact: Whenever Barracuda (or any consumer) falls 32 messages behind — which is easy during a zone-list refresh, an event-log upload, or a partition-status burst — the very next producer message wipes all 32 queued messages instead of losing just one. The owner sees whole batches of web-UI updates vanish: a zone list that comes back half-populated, a status page that never refreshes, an event log with holes — with no error anywhere, because the send that caused the wipe reports success. The flush loop can additionally stall the producer for up to maxmsg x 100 ms.
evidence: tuxedo 0x5a78e0-0x5a7934 (osal_MqSend attr compare and flush call), 0x5a7694-0x5a7720 (osal_MqFlush drain loop, no early break, 100 ms per iteration via osal_MqRecv(...,0x64,0)), 0x5a786c (same in osal_MqSendPriority), 0x141764-0x141774 and 0x14172c-0x141740 (queue depths 32 for /Q_ServCmdTrsmtr and /Q_ServCmdRcver), 246-caller xref for _Z11osal_MqSendiPci. refutation_attempted: (1) I checked whether osal_MqFlush might be a no-op or drain only one message — it loops on mq_maxmsg from the attributes and memsets each buffer, so it genuinely discards everything. (2) I checked whether the queues are created O_NONBLOCK such that a plain mq_send would fail anyway (making the flush a deliberate 'newest wins' policy): osal_MqCreate is called with the bNonBlock argument = 0 for these queues, so a plain blocking mq_send was available and would have been the safe choice. (3) I checked whether the flush is only used on a queue nobody cares about — it is on the generic primitive used by 246 call sites including the security-status and zone paths. What I could not determine from static analysis alone is how often the 32-deep queue actually fills in practice; the severity below reflects that uncertainty.
fixable_how: Needs a firmware patch (use blocking mq_send, or drop only the oldest single message). No client-side workaround; the only mitigation the owner has is to avoid driving bursts (e.g. not requesting a full zone list and an event-log upload simultaneously).

title: osal_MqSend's timed variant reports ETIMEDOUT as SUCCESS, so th_readEcp silently drops ECP frames from the panel and its own error print never fires
detail:
`osal_MqSend(int,char*,int,int)` at 0x5a79ac builds an absolute deadline of {time(NULL) + 0 sec, arg4 * 1,000,000 ns} and calls mq_timedsend. On failure it fetches errno and at 0x5a7a18 does `cmp r3,#0x6e` (110 = ETIMEDOUT); if errno IS ETIMEDOUT it falls into 0x5a7a20 `mov r0,#0` and returns 0 — the same value it returns on success. Only a non-ETIMEDOUT errno propagates -1.

`th_readEcp` (0x59ce08) is the thread that reads raw ECP frames off /dev/spi. It reads 128 bytes (0x59ce58), stores the length at offset 128 of the 130-byte SEcpMessage (0x59cea4 `strh r4,[fp,#-0x16]`), and posts it with r3 = 0 as the timeout argument (0x59ce84 `mov r3,#0`, still live at the call at 0x59ceac) — an absolute deadline already in the past. So when `/mqRead_ECP_Input` (created at 0x59ddc0-0x59ddc8 with msgsize 0x82 and maxmsg 0x20 = 32) is full, mq_timedsend returns ETIMEDOUT immediately, the wrapper turns that into 0, and the caller's `cmn r0,#1 / bne` (0x59ceb0) treats it as success. The literal "sg_mqReadEcpInput message send fail" at 0xc6466c is therefore unreachable for the queue-full case.
impact: If the ECP consumer thread (th_processEcpInput, which does the security-status update, CAL forwarding and emulation-screen work) stalls for even a few hundred milliseconds, up to 32 queued panel frames build up and every further frame is thrown away with no log line and no retry. Because panel status in this design is edge-triggered on ECP messages, a dropped F7/FC frame means a missed arm/disarm/zone transition that nothing ever re-requests — stale keypad text, a status that lags reality, or an alarm state the web UI never learns about. It is also invisible on the serial console, which makes it very hard for the owner to diagnose.
evidence: tuxedo 0x5a79ac-0x5a7a24 (osal_MqSend 4-arg; 0x5a7a18 `cmp r3,#0x6e`, 0x5a7a20 `mov r0,#0`), 0x59ce84 (`mov r3,#0` timeout arg) and 0x59ceac (call) in th_readEcp, 0x59ceb0-0x59ceb8 (caller's success test and the unreachable error print at 0xc6466c), 0x59ddc0-0x59ddc8 (/mqRead_ECP_Input created msgsize 0x82, maxmsg 0x20). refutation_attempted: (1) I checked whether masking ETIMEDOUT might be deliberate 'best effort' semantics that some other caller depends on — all 11 callers of the 4-arg form (th_readEcp, HandleZoneListResponse, apl_sendEcpConsoleModeData, CVoice::SendMessage, the apl_* test helpers) treat -1 as the only failure, so none of them can distinguish a drop. (2) I checked whether an already-expired absolute deadline would break the normal (non-full) case — POSIX applies the timeout only when the message cannot be queued immediately, so the happy path is unaffected; the bug is purely the misreported failure. (3) I verified th_readEcp really passes 0 and that r3 is not reloaded between 0x59ce84 and the call. (4) I confirmed the queue is 32 deep rather than unbounded, so the full condition is reachable. I could not measure how often the consumer actually falls 32 frames behind on real hardware.
fixable_how: Needs a firmware patch: return -1 (or a distinct drop code) on ETIMEDOUT, and/or give th_readEcp a real timeout so it blocks briefly instead of dropping. No client-side workaround. A partial diagnostic aid available today: watch mq_curmsgs on /mqRead_ECP_Input from a shell to see whether it is pinned at 32.

title: The web-facing per-partition status poller is unreachable: CReceiverThread::getPartitionDetails is dead code, so sltPartitionDetailReqTimeout is never connected and RequestPartitionStatus is only ever driven by the local touchscreen
detail:
`CReceiverThread::getPartitionDetails(char*)` at 0x140480 is the only place that creates the partition-detail poll timer (0x140510 `new CTimer2(0x61)`), connects it (0x140538-0x140544: connect(g_TimerThread, SIGNAL(sigWebStatusReq()), this, SLOT(sltPartitionDetailReqTimeout()))), sets its 2000 ms interval, starts it, and tail-jumps into the slot (0x140568 `b #0x140310`). It is also the only writer of the partition-id array at [this+0x248] (0x1404a8).

A whole-image scan of every PT_LOAD segment of tuxedo for (a) any B or BL, conditional or not, targeting 0x140480 and (b) any 4-byte data word equal to 0x140480, returns nothing. The connect() signature strings are equally isolated: a scan for references to "2sigWebStatusReq()" (0x5daa58) and "1sltPartitionDetailReqTimeout()" (0x5daa6c) finds exactly one literal-pool reference each, both inside getPartitionDetails itself (0x1405c8, 0x1405cc). The bare name string "sltPartitionDetailReqTimeout()" exists only once more, at 0x614bf0, which is the moc metaobject signature table (dispatch by index, not by name).

Consequently the slot is only reachable through qt_static_metacall (0x56aaf8), which requires a connection or an invokeMethod that no code performs. And `RequestPartitionStatus(int,bool)` at 0x585c28 has exactly two BL callers: this dead-connected slot (0x14044c) and `CGo2Partition::sltStatusReqTimeout()` (0xac778) — the local touchscreen's Go-To-Partition screen.

As a secondary observation, if the function were ever wired up it would also leak: 0x1404a0 osal_Malloc's a new array straight into [this+0x248] at 0x1404a8 without freeing the previous one, and it does not reset the function-local static index `i32Idx` (0xd2f484) that sltPartitionDetailReqTimeout uses to walk the array, so a re-issued partition list would resume mid-iteration and skip partitions.
impact: Nothing in the web/remote path ever polls the panel for per-partition status. The only code that asks is the local touchscreen's partition screen, so the panel-derived partition data the web API serves is refreshed only as a side effect of somebody standing at the keypad. For a multi-partition owner this shows up as partition status in the web UI that is stale or never populates, and it is a second, independent reason (beyond the already-documented empty-cache default) that the remote view disagrees with the panel.
evidence: tuxedo 0x140480-0x140568 (getPartitionDetails: malloc into [this+0x248], CTimer2(0x61) creation, connect to sigWebStatusReq/sltPartitionDetailReqTimeout, setInterval 0x7d0, start, tail-jump to 0x140310); exhaustive branch+dataword scan of all PT_LOAD segments finds zero references to 0x140480; literal-reference scan finds 0x5daa58/0x5daa6c used only at 0x1405c8/0x1405cc inside that same function; RequestPartitionStatus (0x585c28) BL xrefs = {0xac778 CGo2Partition::sltStatusReqTimeout, 0x14044c CReceiverThread::sltPartitionDetailReqTimeout}; sltPartitionDetailReqTimeout's only BL caller is qt_static_metacall at 0x56aaf8. title: CReceiverThread::registerclient() flushes the whole tuxedo-to-Barracuda queue, and client presence is tracked by two global booleans, so a second web client breaks the first
detail:
`CReceiverThread::registerclient()` at 0x13c2f8 begins by calling `osal_MqFlush(mpl_msqIdSendToServer)` (0x13c304-0x13c308) — the tuxedo-to-Barracuda /Q_ServCmdTrsmtr queue (32 x 556 bytes, created at 0x141764) — before composing and sending its registration reply. Every SERV_CLIENT_REGISTER (cmd 500) therefore throws away every response and status broadcast already queued for whatever client was connected. The constructors do the same at 0x141754/0x141788 and 0x141b58/0x141b8c.

Client bookkeeping is not a count. `clients_connected` (0xd2f268) and `F7_Mesgs_enabled` (0xd2f269) are single bytes. `unregisterclient()` at 0x13c00c unconditionally zeroes both plus [this+8], with no per-session accounting — so any one client unregistering turns off raw console/keypad forwarding for all of them. `F7_Mesgs_enabled` is the gate at the very top of `wsltHandleRawDataFromPanel` (0x13da04-0x13da20: if the byte is 0, return immediately without forwarding the keypad display data), and it is also cleared by `home_back_press()` (0x13c030-0x13c038), i.e. by any Home/Back press from any session.
impact: The web interface is effectively single-client. Opening the panel's web UI in a second browser, tab, or phone silently wipes the first one's queued updates and the two then fight over the shared F7 flag: pressing Back or Home in one session, or closing one session, stops the live keypad display in the other. For an owner who keeps a browser tab open on a desktop and also uses a phone, the symptom is a web UI that intermittently freezes or goes blank with no error.

title: The event-log retrieval state machine retries forever every 20 seconds with no attempt limit and no failure path

CReceiverThread's event-log request state lives at [this+0x50a4]. `setEventIndex()` (0x13e818) issues AskFromPanel(0x53) and sets state 2, or AskFromPanel(0x55) and sets state 3, and in both cases starts the 20-second timer at [this+0x254] (0x13e8d4-0x13e8e8, interval literal 0x4e20 = 20000 ms; the timer object is a CTimer2 with id 0x63 created at 0x13f504-0x13f520).

`panelResponseTimeout()` (0x13e978) stops the timer, then switches on the state: state 2 -> calls setEventIndex() again (0x13e9c0), which re-issues and re-arms; state 3 -> re-issues AskFromPanel(0x55) with the same arguments, writes state = 3 again (0x13ea28-0x13ea30) and restarts the same 20-second timer (0x13ea34-0x13ea3c); any other state -> clears the state and stops the timer. There is no retry counter, no backoff, and no give-up branch. The only exits are the success paths: `wsltEventDescRcvd` (0x13ec08-0x13ec18) and `sltSetEventIndex` (0x13edac-0x13edc4), which zero the state and stop the timer when the panel answers.

title: CalManager::AnalyzeResponse latches the record-delimiter byte once outside the copy loop, so multi-response CAL frames are merged into one mis-sized record
detail:
`CalManager::AnalyzeResponse(unsigned char*, unsigned short, AnalyzedResponse_t*)` at 0x581918 splits a CAL frame into records separated by the 0xFC/0xFD/0xFE class bytes. Each record is 0x82 bytes in the output structure: [0]=record count, [1]=length, [2]=type, [3..]=payload.

The payload copy loop loads the look-ahead byte exactly once, before the loop, at 0x58198c `ldrb r0,[r4,#1]` (raw bytes 0100d4e5). Inside the loop (0x58199c-0x5819dc, raw bytes verified) the delimiter tests at 0x5819b8 `cmp r0,#0xfc` / 0x5819bc `cmpne r0,#0xfe` and 0x5819d0 `cmp r0,#0xfd` all test that same stale r0 — r0 is never reloaded, while the source pointer `ip` and destination `lr` both advance and the byte actually copied comes from `ldrb r2,[ip,#-1]`. The loop's only real exit is therefore `cmpne r1,#0` (the remaining-length counter reaching zero) at 0x5819d4.

As a result the outer record loop at 0x5819e0-0x5819f0 can only iterate again when the length is non-zero at that point, which happens only if the byte immediately after the type byte was itself a delimiter. In every ordinary frame the first record swallows the entire remainder and the loop returns after one record. This is consistent with the consumer: `RequestResponseProcessing` (0x581e40) passes the AnalyzedResponse_t base straight to `HandleCalResponse` (0x581a90), which only ever dispatches record 0.

The record length field at record[1] is a single byte incremented per copied byte, so it also wraps past 255 while the destination pointer keeps advancing.
impact: If the panel ever packs more than one CAL response into a single frame, only the first response's type is dispatched, its reported length covers the whole remainder of the frame, and the second and subsequent responses are handed to the first response's handler as payload bytes. Handlers such as HandleZoneListResponse and HandleUserInformationResponse walk their payload by the reported length, so they would iterate over another response's bytes as if they were their own data — producing wrong zone/user/partition data rather than a clean parse error. For single-response frames, which appear to be the normal case, the parse is correct.
evidence: tuxedo 0x581918-0x581a00 (AnalyzeResponse), with raw bytes dumped for 0x581988-0x5819f4 showing `ldrb r0,[r4,#1]` only at 0x58198c and no reload inside the 0x58199c-0x5819dc loop; 0x5819b8/0x5819bc/0x5819d0 (delimiter tests on stale r0), 0x5819d4 (`cmpne r1,#0`, the real exit), 0x5819e0-0x5819f0 (outer record advance by 0x82); 0x581eac-0x581f00 (HandleCompletedToken: 0x321-byte AnalyzedResponse_t stack buffer at fp-0x321, calls AnalyzeResponse then RequestResponseProcessing); 0x581e40-0x581e74 (RequestResponseProcessing dispatches only record 0). I refuted that myself: the input length is bounded by the 128-byte ECP read in th_readEcp and further checked by ValidateECPMessageLength (0x59cf6c), whose 0xF2/CAL arm requires pMsg[1]+2 <= len, so a single record cannot exceed the buffer. (3) I checked whether the compiler might legitimately hoist the load because the value is provably loop-invariant — it is not; the source pointer advances, so this is a source-level bug (look-ahead read outside the loop). title: All web secrets (login Random, CSRF tokenkey, REST API AES key/IV) come from srand(time(NULL)) + rand() — one wall-clock second of entropy
detail:
random_string() @0x0001d5d4 (Barracuda) calls time(NULL) then srand() on EVERY invocation, then builds the string with rand()%62 over the 62-char alnum table at 0x8b84c. glibc rand() is fully deterministic for a given seed, so the entire output string is a pure function of the current UNIX second. It is the only randomness source used for web secrets. Three consumers:
  (1) LoginResp_service @0x000133dc: random_string(buf,0x20) -> getKeyFromPassword @0x0001d648 (EVP_BytesToKey with aes-256-cbc/md5, salt=NULL, count=1) -> hex-print 16 bytes -> `strb r3,[r7,#0x1f]` writes NUL at index 31. This is emitted as the `Random` response header. That truncation is exactly why Random is 31 hex chars and not 32 — the established observation is explained by this instruction.
  (2) addSessionItem1 @0x0002b444: random_string(sp,0x20) -> getKeyFromPassword -> strcpy into sessItem[i]+5. That stored string is the value returned by getCSRFToken1 @0x0002b3bc and compared by strcmp against the request's `tokenkey`. So the CSRF token is also 31 hex chars derived from time(NULL) at session creation.
  (3) generateKeyForAPI @0x0001d96c: random_string(sp+0xd0,0x20) is the passphrase fed to EVP_BytesToKey to produce the REST API AES-256 key and IV.
A second-order effect: because srand() is re-seeded per call, two random_string() calls in the same second return identical strings.
impact: None of these values is a secret against an attacker who can bound the generating second. Candidate reconstruction is offline and costs one MD5 per second of window. For tokenkey, an attacker who knows roughly when the owner logged in (e.g. because they can see the traffic, or because logins happen at predictable times) has on the order of 10^2-10^4 candidates for the exact 31-char token that authorises every /handlerequest.html command — arm, disarm, keypad keys, panic. For the login `Random`, the challenge in the challenge-response is predictable, so a captured log1=HMAC-SHA512(Random, user+pass) can be cracked offline with no rate limit and no need to guess the nonce.
evidence: Barracuda @0x0001d5d4 random_string: `bl time` -> `bl srand` -> loop `bl rand` / `__aeabi_idivmod #0x3e`; alphabet string at 0x8b84c. getKeyFromPassword @0x0001d648, NUL truncation at 0x0001d704-0x0001d708. LoginResp_service @0x0001340c calls it; `Random` header set at 0x00013464. addSessionItem1 @0x0002b47c. generateKeyForAPI @0x0001d984. Token comparison: handlerequest_html076EF::service @0x0003a3e0-0x0003a454 (json_get "Token" -> strcmp against header/param `tokenkey`).
refutation_attempted: I looked for a second, stronger RNG that might supersede this one: I cross-referenced every caller of random_key and random_string across the whole binary (blxref over all executable sections, manual BL decode). random_key has zero callers (dead code); random_string has exactly four callers, all listed above. I checked whether srand might be called once at startup with a better seed and these calls be harmless — no: srand is inside random_string itself, at 0x0001d5e8, executed on every call. I checked for /dev/urandom or RAND_bytes usage in the auth path — SharkSSL has its own RNG but nothing in LoginResp_service, addSessionItem1 or generateKeyForAPI touches it. The finding survives.
fixable_how: Needs firmware patch (replace random_string with a /dev/urandom read and seed srand at most once). No client-side workaround. Owner-side mitigation: keep the panel off any network segment an untrusted device can reach, and prefer the HTTPS listener so the tokenkey is not also observable on the wire.

title: The REST API AES-256 key and IV are a single global, permanent device secret generated at first boot when the clock is hard-set to 01 Jan 2013
detail:
generateKeyForAPI @0x0001d96c runs once from barracuda() @0x000108b8 at process start. It builds a 31-char passphrase via random_string, derives key+IV with EVP_BytesToKey(aes-256-cbc, md5, salt=NULL, count=1), hex-encodes them as PrivateKey (64 hex) / PublicKey (32 hex), and stores them in a device node whose DeviceMAC is the literal string "Browser" in /opt/tuxedo/configuration/registereddevMAClist.json (written by writeRemoteTuxDevNode @0x0001881c). The function first walks the existing node list and, if a node with DeviceMAC=="Browser" already exists, returns without writing (loop at 0x0001db18-0x0001db50). So the key/IV are generated exactly once, on the first boot where that file has no Browser node, and then persist across reboots forever. They are per-DEVICE, not per-session and not per-user: the same 64+32 hex blob is what every browser reads from `<input id="readit">` on /tuxedoapi.html.
The seed for that one generation is time(NULL) at Barracuda startup. /etc/rc.d/init.d/startup sets the clock before launching anything: if /opt/tuxedo/configuration/datetime is absent it runs `date 0101000013`, i.e. 01 Jan 2013 00:00:00. /opt/tuxedo/configuration/ is empty in the firmware image, so on a factory-fresh unit (or after a config wipe) the key is generated within seconds of a fixed timestamp.
impact: An attacker who recovers this key/IV can encrypt and decrypt every REST API payload and forge the `authtoken` for every endpoint, permanently — logging out, changing the web password, or rebooting does not rotate it. Only a factory reset does. On a first-boot-derived key the offline search space is roughly the number of seconds between `date 0101000013` and Barracuda's start, i.e. tens to a few hundred candidates.
evidence: generateKeyForAPI @0x0001d96c (random_string 0x0001d984, EVP_BytesToKey 0x0001da04, %02x hex loops at 0x0001da1c and 0x0001da48, "PrivateKey"/"PublicKey" json_new_a at 0x0001dae4/0x0001daf8); Browser-node existence check 0x0001db18-0x0001db50; writeRemoteTuxDevNode @0x0001881c writing /opt/tuxedo/configuration/registereddevMAClist.json (string at 0x8b29c). Startup clock default: fw/carved/app2_root/etc/rc.d/init.d/startup, `date 0101000013` in the else branch of the /opt/tuxedo/configuration/datetime test. Empty config dir: fw/carved/app2_root/opt/tuxedo/configuration/.
refutation_attempted: I tried to show the key is per-session: it is read by the browser from `readit` on the tuxedoapi page, so it could plausibly be re-minted per login. It is not — generateKeyForAPI is called only from barracuda()+0x1b8 (single BL xref across the whole binary) and short-circuits when a "Browser" node exists, so no login path can rotate it. I also tried to show the file ships pre-populated (which would mean a factory-set key rather than a first-boot-derived one): opt/tuxedo/configuration/ is empty in the extracted rootfs. The one thing I could not determine is whether that directory lives on a separate JFFS2 volume not present in this carve, so the exact seed window on this owner's unit is unverified — that part I mark LIKELY, the global/permanent scoping is CONFIRMED.
fixable_how: Needs firmware patch. Owner-side partial mitigation: a factory reset performed while the panel's clock is correct (NTP-synced, so /opt/tuxedo/configuration/datetime exists) widens the seed window considerably, but the key is still time-seeded and still global.

title: The REST API `authtoken` is a static per-endpoint value that covers neither the request body nor any nonce — capture once, replay forever
detail: tuxapi.js builds authtoken as CryptoJS.HmacSHA1("MACID:Browser,Path:API_REV01/<endpoint>", api_key_enc) where api_key_enc is the global device key from finding 2. The HMAC input is a constant string per endpoint. The POST body is `param=<b64 AES ciphertext>&len=<len>&tstamp=` + Math.random() — tstamp is not a timestamp at all, it is a random float, and it is not covered by the HMAC. The `identity` header is simply the IV hex, also global.
impact: Every request to a given endpoint carries the same authtoken for the life of the device. Anyone who observes one API call (see finding 5 — a plain-HTTP listener exists) obtains a permanent credential for that endpoint that survives password changes, logout and reboot. There is no replay window to close because there is no replay protection: the same body can be resent indefinitely. With the key itself (finding 2) the attacker mints tokens for every other endpoint too.
evidence: webapp/script/tuxapi.js line 71 and ~40 similar sites: `var header = "MACID:Browser,Path:" + hPath + "/<endpoint>"; callAPI_POST(url, dataCnt, dataCnt.length, CryptoJS.HmacSHA1(header, api_key_enc));`. callAPI_POST at tuxapi.js:945-953 sets headers authtoken and identity and sends `"param=" + data + "&len=" + paramlength + "&tstamp=" + Math.random()`. Key/IV read at tuxapi.js:5-6 from `document.getElementById("readit").value`. Format string for the readit input: Barracuda 0x0053b6a4 `<input type="hidden" id="readit" value="%s%s">`. Server-side token strings "MACID:" @0x00086b30 and ",Path:" @0x00086b38.
refutation_attempted: I looked for server-side replay defence that the JS would not show: I searched the binary for a nonce/timestamp store or a monotonic counter checked against `tstamp`, and for any per-session component in the token. The only per-request inputs are the endpoint path and the global key; `tstamp` is a jQuery-side cache-buster with no server-side symbol consuming it. I also considered that the session cookie might be additionally required on /system_http_api — the vendor's own documentation strings (e.g. 0x0007ea00) say the authtoken header is the authentication mechanism and is "Not applicable for browser clients", implying browser clients are authorised by session instead; I could not locate the /system_http_api dispatcher to prove which check is applied, so the exact severity for a token-only (cookie-less) attacker is UNKNOWN. The static-token property itself is CONFIRMED from the client code and the server-side MACID/Path strings.
fixable_how: Needs firmware patch (bind the HMAC to body, method and a server-verified nonce). No client-side workaround.

title: No per-command authorisation on /handlerequest.html — any valid session may invoke any cmd, and the URL ACL table is Barracuda's leftover demo data
detail: handlerequest_html076EF::service @0x0003a2a0 does exactly three checks before dispatching: (a) a session/locality gate at 0x0003a388-0x0003a3b8, (b) getCSRFToken1(sessionid) must be non-NULL, (c) strcmp of the stored Token against the `tokenkey` header or query parameter (0x0003a3cc-0x0003a454). It then falls straight into the `Type` switch at 0x0003a48c. Across the whole 17988-byte function there is not a single call to AuthenticatedUser_*, MyUserDB_user2Roles, or any role/level accessor. Separately, the realm's authoriser MySecurityRealm_authorize @0x0001dcb4 walks a 5-entry table at securityDB (0x0008b8b8) whose path prefixes are Barracuda's shipped sample data — "family/dad", "family/mom", "family/kids", "family" — and returns 1 (ALLOW) when the loop exhausts without a prefix match (0x0001dd7c). No real panel URL begins with "family", so the authoriser allows everything. MyUserDB_user2Roles @0x00014a50 is a two-instruction stub that returns the constant 1.

Any account that can log in — including a low-privilege one — can drive every command code: arm/disarm (1-4), multi-partition arming (6-9, 25-29), console keypad mode (19, which forwards raw keypresses including the A/B/C/D panic keys), camera and scene commands. The only thing standing between a logged-in low-privilege user and a disarm is the 4-digit panel user code, which the panel validates over ECP, not the web layer.

title: The alarm user code (uCode) travels in a GET query string over a plain-HTTP listener
detail: Every panel command is issued as `GET /handlerequest.html?cmd=..&Type=..&pID=..&uCode=<4-digit user code>&sessionid=<id>&filters=0&index=0&tarTemp=0&tokenkey=<31 hex>&sid=<random>`. The user code the operator types into the keypad dialog is placed verbatim into `uCode` (armcontrolscript.js copies the value of hidUserCode into hiduCode and passes it to sendCommand). The mobile variant does the same with `usercode=`. Barracuda opens two non-TLS HttpServCon listeners in addition to the SharkSSL one, and the vendor's own API documentation strings use http:// URLs, so the LAN traffic is not necessarily encrypted.
impact: A passive attacker on the LAN (ARP-spoofing, a switch SPAN port, a compromised IoT device, or just Wi-Fi) recovers three things from one captured arm/disarm: the panel user code in cleartext, the sessionid, and the tokenkey. That triple is everything needed to disarm the alarm at will for the life of the session. The user code additionally lands in any intermediate proxy log and in the browser's network/devtools history. This is the single most practical attack on a LAN the owner otherwise controls.
evidence: webapp/script/httpRequest.js:18 and webapp/script/HomehttpRequest.js:19 build the URL with `&uCode=` + uCode; webapp/script/mobile/script/connect.js:13 uses /handlerequest_mobile.html?...&usercode=. Code entry -> parameter: webapp/script/armcontrolscript.js:221,235 (hiduCode = pass) and :303 (sendCommand(...,document.getElementById("hiduCode").value,...)). Server side reads it as a plain parameter: handlerequest service @0x0003a960 and 0x0003a9a4 `HttpRequest_getParameter("uCode")` -> U32_atoi. Plain listeners: openSocketCon @0x0000c848 constructs two HttpServCon (0x0000c938, 0x0000c990) plus HttpSharkSslServCon; doc strings such as 0x0007eb58 give http:// examples.

title: The (sessionid, tokenkey) pair is a cookie-less bearer credential, and the session cookie is set without HttpOnly or Secure
detail:
The session gate in handlerequest_html076EF::service @0x0003a388-0x0003a3b8 evaluates two booleans: whether a Barracuda session exists (HttpRequest_getSession(req,0), NULL when no valid cookie) and a locality/login flag. It denies ONLY the case (no session AND flag set). With no session cookie at all and a same-subnet client while localLoginStatus is 0, execution falls through to the token check, and the sessionid used for the token lookup is then taken from the *query parameter* rather than the server-side session (the value at [sp,#0x78] is overwritten by the session's own id only when a session exists, at 0x0003a33c). So possession of the sessionid and tokenkey values alone is sufficient — no cookie required.
Separately, HttpRequest_getSession @0x00071aac creates the session cookie with HttpCookie_setValue, HttpCookie_setPath("/") and HttpCookie_activate, and calls neither a secure nor an HttpOnly setter, even though Barracuda has "; HttpOnly" (0x0053f3f0) and "; secure" (0x0053f3fc) in its cookie formatter. The cookie name is sprintf("z9ZAqJtI_%u", time(NULL)) fixed at process start (0x0000c6fc) — not random per login as previously assumed — and the same start timestamp is echoed into the login page as `var server="..."` (login_shtml service @0x000383e8 getServerStartTime, format string 0x00537c20). The cookie VALUE is HttpSession_fmtSessionId @0x00071100 = hex(session->id) ++ hex(session->creationTime), where session->id = baGetMsClock() * 0x75BCD15 (0x00071988-0x00071998) and creationTime = time(NULL).
impact: Three consequences. (1) The credential lives in URLs, so it leaks anywhere URLs leak — proxy logs, packet captures, devtools — and is not protected by cookie-scoping rules. (2) No HttpOnly means any script that runs in the panel's origin reads the session cookie; no Secure means the browser will send it over the plain-HTTP listener even after an HTTPS login. (3) The session id is not random: 0x75BCD15 is odd, so the multiply is a bijection mod 2^32 and any single observed sessionid inverts to the device's exact millisecond uptime. An attacker holding one legitimate low-privilege session can therefore compute the panel's clock and enumerate a narrow window of candidate ids for another session, and the second half of the cookie is simply the login's UNIX second.
evidence: Gate: 0x0003a2e8/0x0003a2f8 HttpRequest_getSession(req,0); 0x0003a33c overwrite of [sp,#0x78]; branch logic 0x0003a388-0x0003a3b8; token lookup 0x0003a3bc getCSRFToken1([sp,#0x78]); tokenkey accepted from header (0x0003a3d0) or query parameter (0x0003a414). Cookie creation without flags: 0x00071ab4-0x00071ae8. Cookie name: 0x0000c6ec-0x0000c708 ('z9ZAqJtI_%u'). Session id derivation: 0x00071988 baGetMsClock, 0x00071990 literal 0x75bcd15, 0x00071998 mul. fmtSessionId: 0x00071100.
refutation_attempted: I specifically tried to prove classic session fixation, and failed — HttpRequest_getSession never adopts a client-supplied id; it looks the cookie value up in a splay tree and mints its own id on miss. So fixation is NOT a finding here and I am not reporting it. I re-derived the ARM condition codes at 0x0003a3a0-0x0003a3b8 (rsbs/movlo giving r3 = !r0) twice by hand to be sure the cookie-less case really falls through rather than denying; the deny target 0x0003e85c is reachable only from the (no session, flag set) combination. What I could NOT confirm is how narrow the id search window is in practice, because that depends on how tightly an attacker can bound the victim's login instant — the id-inversion property is CONFIRMED, the practical prediction attack I would rate LIKELY.
fixable_how: Needs firmware patch for the cookie flags, the id source and moving the token out of URLs. Owner-side: use HTTPS only, and do not browse the panel from a machine that also runs untrusted code.

title: When LocalLogin is 0, any host on the panel's /24 gets full pages, a session and a tokenkey with no credentials at all
detail: Every page handler follows the same pattern. armcontrol_html076EF::service @0x000445b8: if no session exists and checkforlocalremote(req) returns 0, it sets r6 = getLocalLoginStatus(); then `cmp r6,#1; bne` — the AuthenticatedUser_get1 check and the redirect to /authenticated/index.html happen ONLY when r6 == 1. Any other value renders the page, which embeds hidSession and hiddenKey (eventHandler.js:1260-1261 expose them as getSessionIDFromEV/getKeyFromEV). localLoginStatus is loaded by setLoginForLocal @0x0002bf50 from /opt/tuxedo/configuration/Tuxedo.json, key BARRACUDA[0].LocalLogin (json_get at 0x0002c044), defaulting to 1 only if the file cannot be opened (0x0002bf94). checkforlocalremote @0x0002ddd0 is not a netmask test: it sprintf's the peer IP and boardIP to 11 chars each, copies characters until the third dot, and strcmp's — i.e. a first-three-octets string comparison.
impact: If the owner has the panel's 'login required for local access' setting off, an unauthenticated device on the same /24 can load armcontrol.html / consolekeypad.html / home.html, harvest sessionid and tokenkey directly from the HTML, and then issue commands. Arming (Type=1/2) with uCode=0 is forwarded with the 0xffff placeholder (0x0003a998), and console mode (Type=19) forwards raw keypresses — including the A/B/C/D panic keys, which on a Honeywell panel require no user code and will signal fire/police/medical. Disarm still needs a valid code. The /24 heuristic also means a flat 10.0.0.0/8 or 192.168.0.0/16 LAN is only partially covered by the 'local' test, in both directions.
evidence: armcontrol_html076EF::service @0x000445b8: getSession 0x000445ec, checkforlocalremote 0x00044610, getLocalLoginStatus 0x0004461c, `cmp r6,#1 / bne 0x449ec` at 0x00044628-0x00044630, AuthenticatedUser_get1 + redirect to '/authenticated/index.html?url=armcontrol.html' at 0x00044638-0x00044648. Same getLocalLoginStatus call appears at the head of home, console, consolekeypad, index, mobileview, devicelist, occupancy, groups, camerasetup, scene_configuration, videoscreen, camsingleview, camaddedit, videoplayback, zwavedevicelist and eventhandler services. setLoginForLocal @0x0002bf50; 'LocalLogin' string 0x0008f568. checkforlocalremote @0x0002ddd0 (two %.*s sprintf with width 11 at 0x0002de44/0x0002de58, dot-counting loops, strcmp at 0x0002ded0). Panic keys: webapp/script/consoleRequest.js createButtons maps btnA/B/C/D to panicButtonPress -> sendCommand(SERV_CONSOLE_MODE=19,...).
refutation_attempted: I tried to show the pages still gate on something else after rendering — they do not; the AuthenticatedUser check is inside the `r6 == 1` arm only, and the fall-through at 0x000449ec leads to page rendering. I tried to establish the shipped default for LocalLogin so I could say whether this is live on the owner's unit: Tuxedo.json is not present in the extracted rootfs (opt/tuxedo/configuration is empty), so the effective default is UNKNOWN — the code default when the file is missing is 1 (login required), which is the safe value, so this bites only if the setting has been turned off. I state that explicitly rather than assuming the worst.
fixable_how: Config change, no firmware patch needed: set the panel's local-access login requirement on (Tuxedo.json BARRACUDA.LocalLogin = 1) so the page handlers take the authenticated branch.

title: Type=501 is processed on the authorisation-failure path — unauthenticated, off-subnet clients can inject a message into the panel application
detail: When the session/locality gate in handlerequest_html076EF::service denies a request it branches to 0x0003e85c, which is not a plain error return: it compares Type against 0x1F5 (501) and, on a match, jumps to 0x0003e648, which reads the `sessionid` parameter, writes command 0x1F7 (503, SERV_HOME) into the message struct and calls osal_MqSend to the tuxedo application. This happens BEFORE and INSTEAD OF the getCSRFToken1 / tokenkey comparison, so no session, no cookie and no token are required.
impact: An unauthenticated client — including one that fails the same-subnet check, i.e. a genuinely remote one — can send a HOME command into the panel's message queue. Practically that pushes the touchscreen back to its Home screen. Low direct harm, but it is a real pre-authentication path into the panel's IPC, it is a reliable liveness/existence oracle for the panel, and repeated use would make the touchscreen unusable.
evidence: handlerequest_html076EF::service deny target 0x0003e85c: `ldr r3,=0x1f5; cmp r5,r3; bne 0x3e680; b 0x3e648`. At 0x0003e648: HttpRequest_getParameter("sessionid") -> U32_atoi -> stored at [sp,#0xabc]; literal 0x1f7 stored at [sp,#0xac0] (0x0003e668-0x0003e674); osal_MqSend with length 0x194 at 0x0003e678. The token check at 0x0003a3bc is never reached on this path.
refutation_attempted: I checked whether the 0x194-byte message buffer might leak stack contents to the panel app on this path — it does not; both branches memset it to zero first (0x0003a340 and 0x0003a368), so this is a clean, bounded message and not a memory-disclosure primitive. I also checked whether 0x0003e85c is reachable in normal operation, i.e. whether this is dead code: it is the target of the `beq` at 0x0003a3b8, reached whenever there is no session and the locality/login flag is set, which is exactly the unauthenticated-remote case. Survives, but I have kept the severity honest — the payload is a single navigation command.
fixable_how: Needs firmware patch (move the Type==501 special case behind the token check).

title: 'Remember Password' encrypts the stored credentials with a key printed in the login page, and a legacy login page stores them in cleartext cookies
detail: validatelogin.js, when the persistentCookie box is ticked, sets cookies data1 (username) and data2 (password) for 365 days, AES-CBC encrypted with CryptoJS.enc.Hex.parse(reqStrLen) as key and reqStrLen1 as IV. Both reqStrLen and reqStrLen1 are built by repeating the page-global `server` string until they reach 32 and 16 hex characters. `server` is not a secret: login_shtml076EF::service @0x0003835c emits `var login="%s";var myID="%s";var timeOut=%d;var server="%s";` with the fourth argument taken from getServerStartTime() @0x0002df3c — the Barracuda process start time, printed in plaintext in the login page HTML and also embedded in the session cookie NAME (z9ZAqJtI_<same timestamp>). The cookies are set with the bare `document.cookie = name + "=" + value` helper, so no HttpOnly, no Secure, no SameSite. Separately, webapp/script/login.js (an older login page) writes cookies 'userName', 'userPassword' and 'latestuserpwd' ("user:pass") with no encryption at all.
impact: Anyone who can read the browser's cookie jar for the panel origin — a shared computer, a browser-data stealer, or any script running in the panel's origin given the missing HttpOnly flag — recovers the web account password in plaintext, because the decryption key is published on the login page of the same server. The 365-day lifetime means it persists long after the session does.
evidence: webapp/script/validatelogin.js: key/IV construction from `server.toString()` repeated to 32/16 chars, then setCookie("data1", encryptData(username, reqStrLen, reqStrLen1), 365) and setCookie("data2", encryptData(password, ...), 365); encryptData() uses CryptoJS.AES with mode CBC and ZeroPadding; getHeightWidth() reverses it on page load. setCookie() at the bottom of the same file writes a bare document.cookie with no flags. Server side: login_shtml076EF::service @0x000383e8 `bl getServerStartTime`, format string at 0x00537c20. Cleartext variant: webapp/script/login.js SetCookie('userName',...), SetCookie('userPassword',...), SetCookie('latestuserpwd', userName+":"+userPassword, 24*60).
refutation_attempted: I tried to show `server` is a per-device secret that an attacker would not have — it is the opposite: the login page literally prints it, and the session cookie name discloses the same timestamp on every response, so the key is available to anyone who can reach the panel at all. I also tried to confirm whether login.js (the cleartext variant) is still wired up: it belongs to the older login2.html flow, which posts a bare hex_md5(user+pass) as `log` to /authenticated/index.html rather than the current HMAC-SHA512 scheme, so it is probably a dead legacy page — whether the server still accepts that old `log` format is UNKNOWN and I did not want to assert it. The validatelogin.js finding does not depend on that and stands on its own.
fixable_how: Client-side workaround available now: never tick 'Remember Password', and clear the data1/data2 cookies for the panel origin if it was ever ticked. Fixing the scheme itself needs a firmware patch.

title: HTTPS listener presents the SharkSSL vendor DEMO certificate, and its 1024-bit RSA private key is compiled into /opt/webserver/Barracuda
detail:
The Barracuda binary contains the object sharkSslDemoCertSrv at VA 0x853b1, 1152 bytes (from .symtab). Bytes 0..692 are a DER X.509 certificate; bytes 693..1151 are the matching RSA private key in SharkSSL's raw format (11-byte header 'ffffff00 0400 8000 00010001', where 0x0400=1024 bits and 0x00010001=e=65537, followed by 448 bytes = a 128-byte modulus plus five 64-byte CRT parameters p,q,dP,dQ,qInv). Certificate details parsed from the DER: subject/issuer O='Real Time Logic', OU='SharkSSL', CN='server demo 1024 bits' issued by CN='demo CA', emailAddress=ginfo@realtimelogic.com, L='Laguna Niguel'; signature algorithm OID 1.2.840.113549.1.1.4 = md5WithRSAEncryption; validity 090827144047Z to 190825144047Z (2009-08-27 to 2019-08-25). A companion trust anchor sharkSslCAList (740 bytes @0x85831) holds the matching 'demo CA'. This is the demo credential shipped in the SharkSSL / Barracuda App Server source distribution, i.e. the same key is in every copy of that SDK and in every Tuxedo of this firmware.

Usage is not incidental. The 4-byte literal 0x000853b1 appears at VA 0xcb2c, which is inside the literal pool of _Z13openSocketConP10HttpServerP6SoDispiss (@0xc848, size 756 — range 0xc848..0xcb3c). Both code paths load it into r2 immediately before calling SharkSsl_constructor: 'ldr r2,[pc,#0x138]' @0xc9ec (0xc9ec+8+0x138 = 0xcb2c) then 'bl #0x4b070 ; SharkSsl_constructor' @0xca00; and 'ldr r2,[pc,#0xb0]' @0xca74 (= 0xcb2c) then the same call @0xca84. Each branch then calls HttpSharkSslServCon_constructor (@0x49d84) to stand up the TLS listener. openSocketCon is called twice from barracuda() (@0x108dc with r2=0x50=80, and @0x10900).
impact: Every Tuxedo Touch on this firmware terminates HTTPS with a key that anyone can extract from a public SDK or from this firmware image in about a minute. Passive decryption of the whole session is trivial (the enabled RSA-static suites have no forward secrecy), and active impersonation of the panel is trivial. That directly exposes the authentication material the owner has already mapped: the Random / RandomID challenge, log=HMAC-SHA512(Random, user) and log1=HMAC-SHA512(Random, user+pass) POST, the per-session cookie, and above all the readit blob from /tuxedoapi.html (64 hex chars of AES-256 key + 32 hex chars of IV) that protects every subsequent API call. It equally exposes uCode / sessionid / tokenkey on the /handlerequest.html security API — i.e. arm, disarm, and user codes. The certificate also expired on 2019-08-25 and is MD5-signed with a 1024-bit key, so every modern browser hard-fails it, which trains the owner to click through the warning and destroys any chance of noticing a real MITM.
evidence: C:\Users\dev\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\D--PersonalProjects-iot-protocol-tools\000ba43d-52f5-43a6-902d-6c0edfdf3ceb\scratchpad\fw\carved\app2_root\opt\webserver\Barracuda — .symtab sharkSslDemoCertSrv @0x853b1 size 1152; sharkSslCAList @0x85831 size 740; _Z13openSocketConP10HttpServerP6SoDispiss @0xc848 size 756; literal 0x000853b1 at file offset 0x4b2c = VA 0xcb2c; SharkSsl_constructor @0x4b070 called @0xca00 and @0xca84 with r2 = that literal; HttpSharkSslServCon_constructor @0x49d84; string 'Failed to run Barracuda in HTTPS port %d'; build path /home/george/tux/webserver5.3.21.0/Webserver5.3.21.0/src/plugins/SharkSSL/src/SharkSslCert.c. Cert bytes dumped to scratchpad\demoCertSrv.bin / demo.der.
refutation_attempted: Four attempts to kill this. (1) I looked for a per-device certificate that would override the compiled-in demo: `find` across the whole rootfs for *.pem, *.crt, *.key, *.der and any filename containing 'cert' returned nothing outside libxml2 documentation — there is no certificate file on the image at all. (2) I checked whether the demo cert pointer might be a fallback in a branch that is normally not taken: it is not — BOTH arms of openSocketCon's if/else load the same literal 0xcb2c into r2 before SharkSsl_constructor, so there is no non-demo path in that function. (3) I checked whether the cert blob might be certificate-only with the key loaded separately: the 1152-byte object is 693 bytes of DER plus 459 bytes that decompose exactly as an RSA-1024 private key with CRT parameters (11 + 128 + 5*64 = 459), and the header encodes 0x0400 bits and e=0x00010001 — it is a full private key. (4) I checked whether Barracuda might actually be doing TLS through OpenSSL instead, which would make the SharkSSL cert dead code: Barracuda's .dynsym imports no SSL_*, SSLv23_*, or TLSv1_* symbol at all, only EVP_/HMAC_/BIO_, so SharkSSL is unambiguously the TLS implementation. What I could NOT determine from the image alone is whether the HTTPS listener is on by default or only after the owner enables remote access — openSocketCon builds it unconditionally, but the port and flag arguments come from configuration I cannot read statically. That caveat does not affect the key-in-binary fact.
fixable_how: Not fixable in configuration and not fixable client-side — the key is compiled into the binary and there is no certificate file to replace. Requires a firmware patch from Honeywell that generates a per-device key at first boot (none is coming; this platform is long EOL). Owner mitigation: treat the panel's HTTPS as equivalent to cleartext. Put it on an isolated VLAN/SSID, allow inbound 80/443 only from named hosts, never port-forward it, and if remote access is needed put it behind a reverse proxy or VPN that terminates a real certificate. If you write your own client, pin the expected demo cert so at least you detect substitution — but do not treat the channel as confidential.

WHAT IS *NOT* THERE (refutations of the usual assumptions about this device — I checked because these would otherwise dominate the risk):
- No dropbear, no sshd, no telnetd, no boa, no smbd, no inetd binary exists anywhere in the image. /etc/rc.d/init.d/{dropbear,sshd,inetd,boa,smb} all begin with "if [ ! -x <binary> ] then exit 0". /etc/inetd.conf does list telnet -> /usr/sbin/telnetd, but that binary is absent and inetd is never started.
- /etc/rc.d/rc.conf: cfg_services="mount-proc-sys udev hostname depmod modules filesystems" — inetd, portmap, dropbear, sshd, boa, smb, dhcpd are all in all_services but NOT in cfg_services, and /etc/rc.d/rcS only iterates cfg_services. /sbin/portmap exists but is never launched. So no NFS/rpc surface either, despite rpc.mountd/rpc.nfsd/rpc.statd shipping in /usr/sbin.
- /tuxedo has DT_NEEDED libminiupnpc.so.4 but imports NONE of that library's 39 exported symbols — the link is stale. I found no evidence of UPnP-IGD port forwarding (UPNP_AddPortMapping) from any shipped binary, so I do not claim the panel punches its own hole in the router.

FIREWALL PRIORITY FOR THE OWNER (highest first):
1. TCP 80 and 443 on the panel — put the panel on an isolated VLAN/SSID and allow inbound only from the specific hosts that need it. Never port-forward these from the Internet. The HTTPS side gives essentially no confidentiality against anyone who has the firmware (see finding 1), and the HTTP side gives none at all.
2. Outbound HTTPS to tccaps.honeywell.com from the panel — certificate validation is off (finding 2); anyone on-path can impersonate the cloud. Block it if the thermostat cloud feature is unused.
3. UDP 5353 (avahi + mDNSResponder) — LAN-scope only; drop at any router boundary.
4. Outbound RTSP to IP cameras (finding 6) — keep cameras and panel in the same isolated segment; a compromised camera reaches a 2011 live555.

title: /thermostatclient disables TLS certificate validation entirely for its HTTPS calls to tccaps.honeywell.com
detail: In /thermostatclient, function _Z16perform_http_apiPKcS0_ (perform_http_api(char const*, char const*)) at 0xc050, size 380: 'mov r7, #0' at 0xc0a8 sets r7 to zero and r7 is never reassigned before the two relevant calls. title: OpenSSL 1.0.1h (June 2014), end-of-life since Jan 2017, is the TLS stack for every outbound HTTPS connection the panel makes

The 1.0.1 branch reached end of life on 2016-12-31 and has received no fixes for over nine years. Reachability is specifically as a CLIENT: libcurl 7.35.0 (/usr/lib/libcurl.so.4.3.0) imports the full SSL_CTX_new / SSL_CTX_set_verify / SSL_CTX_load_verify_locations family from this libssl, and libcurl is linked by /opt/webserver/Barracuda, /tuxedo and /thermostatclient. The library also still contains the SSLv2 and SSLv3 method implementations ('SSLv2 part of OpenSSL 1.0.1h', 'SSLv3 part of OpenSSL 1.0.1h'). CVE classes that clearly fall in range for 1.0.1h and are client-relevant: CVE-2014-3566 (POODLE, SSLv3 CBC padding), CVE-2015-0204 (FREAK, export-RSA downgrade), CVE-2015-4000 (Logjam, export-DHE downgrade), CVE-2016-0800 (DROWN, SSLv2 cross-protocol), CVE-2016-2107 (AES-NI CBC MAC-check padding oracle), CVE-2016-2108 (ASN.1 negative-zero memory corruption), plus the August/October 2014 batch CVE-2014-3505/3506/3507/3508/3509/3510/3511/3512 and CVE-2014-3567/3568, all of which postdate 1.0.1h.

Combined with finding 2 (validation switched off for the cloud host) an on-path attacker does not even need an OpenSSL bug for that particular connection.

title: SharkSSL server offers RC4 and 3DES cipher suites on the panel's HTTPS listener
detail: sharkSslCipherSuiteList (.symtab, VA 0x54438c, 208 bytes = 13 entries of 16 bytes) in /opt/webserver/Barracuda. Decoding the 16-bit suite ID at +8 in each entry gives, in server preference order: 0x006B TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA256, 0x0039 DHE_RSA_AES_256_CBC_SHA, 0x009E DHE_RSA_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, 0x0067 DHE_RSA_AES_128_CBC_SHA256, 0x0033 DHE_RSA_AES_128_CBC_SHA, 0x0016 DHE_RSA_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA, 0x003D RSA_AES_256_CBC_SHA256, 0x0035 RSA_AES_256_CBC_SHA, 0x009C RSA_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, 0x003C RSA_AES_128_CBC_SHA256, 0x002F RSA_AES_128_CBC_SHA, 0x000A RSA_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA, 0x0005 TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_SHA. The last three are the problem: RC4 (0x0005) is prohibited by RFC 7465 and biased-keystream recoverable (CVE-2013-2566 / the 'Bar Mitzvah' and RC4 NOMORE classes), and the two 3DES suites (0x000A, 0x0016) are 64-bit block ciphers subject to SWEET32 birthday collision attacks (CVE-2016-2183).
impact: A client that negotiates down — an old browser, a scripted client that does not restrict its cipher list, or an active downgrade — ends up protecting the panel's session with RC4 or 3DES. In practice this is a second-order problem on this device because the certificate key is public anyway (finding 1), so an attacker has an easier route. It matters mainly for anyone who tries to harden this panel by pinning the demo cert and assuming the transport is otherwise sound: it is not, unless the client restricts the suite list.
evidence: C:\Users\dev\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\D--PersonalProjects-iot-protocol-tools\000ba43d-52f5-43a6-902d-6c0edfdf3ceb\scratchpad\fw\carved\app2_root\opt\webserver\Barracuda — .symtab sharkSslCipherSuiteList @0x54438c size 208; raw bytes dumped from file offset 0x53c38c; suite IDs at entry+8 as listed above.
refutation_attempted: I tried to show the list is dead or overridden. (1) Maybe it is a compile-time superset that a runtime call filters: SharkSsl_constructor (@0x4b070) is called from openSocketCon with a stack argument of 0x800 in both branches, which is a buffer size, not a cipher mask, and I found no call to any suite-selection setter. I could not positively prove no filtering happens, which is why I report the list as offered rather than proving RC4 is negotiated in a live handshake. (2) I checked whether the presence of RC4 might be balanced by the stack being TLS1.2-capable, which would let a good client avoid it entirely: it is — 0x009C and 0x009E are AES-GCM/SHA256 suites that only exist in TLS 1.2, so a modern client will not touch RC4. That is a genuine mitigating fact and it is why I rated this medium rather than high, not a refutation of the list's contents. (3) sharkSslProtList @0x544328 is only 4 bytes and reads as ASCII '0123', so it did not give me a protocol-version floor; I therefore do NOT claim SSLv3 is or is not offered.

Client-side workaround: any tool you write against this panel should pin its own cipher list to the AES-GCM or AES-CBC-SHA256 suites and refuse RC4/3DES, so a downgrade fails loudly. Firmware patch would be required to remove them from the server side.

title: live555 v2011.11.02 is the RTSP client for IP cameras, exposed to camera-controlled protocol data
detail: /vidrec/lib/libliveMedia.so.1 carries the version string 'LIVE555 Streaming Media v' followed by '2011.11.02' — a release now roughly fourteen years old. /vidrec/vidApp links it together with libgroupsock.so.1, libUsageEnvironment.so.1 and libBasicUsageEnvironment.so.1, and its .dynsym shows it is a CLIENT: RTSPClient::createNew, RTSPClient::describeURL, RTSPClient::setupMediaSubsession, RTSPClient::playMediaSession, RTSPClient::sendTeardownCommand, MediaSession::createNew, plus local sinks RVUBufferSink and RVU_H264BufferSink. /supervis launches it ('/vidrec/vidApp &'). The attacker-facing surface is therefore the RTSP response path: DESCRIBE responses, SDP parsing in MediaSession, and the RTP/H.264 depacketiser — all fed by whatever the configured camera sends. The 2011 build predates every publicly fixed live555 memory-safety bug of the 2018-2019 era (CVE-2018-4013, CVE-2019-6256, CVE-2019-7314, CVE-2019-9215) and has none of those fixes.
impact: A camera that is compromised, spoofed, or simply hostile (these are commonly cheap devices on the same flat LAN) can feed malformed SDP or RTP to a fourteen-year-old C++ parser running as root on the alarm panel. That is a plausible route from 'one weak camera' to 'code execution on the alarm panel', which is a much worse position than the camera alone.

title: Linux 2.6.31 (2009) and glibc 2.5 (2006) underneath everything, with no post-2017 fixes
detail: The decompressed kernel banner reads 'Linux version 2.6.31-207-g7286c01 (root@optgw2) (gcc version 4.1.2) #1094 PREEMPT Tue Sep 19 11:53:48 UTC 2017'. The build date is 2017 but the source base is upstream 2.6.31, released September 2009 and out of upstream support since 2010; the '-207-g7286c01' suffix is a Freescale/vendor BSP tag, not a stable-tree backport series. Userspace matches: /lib/libc-2.5.so contains 'GNU C Library stable release version 2.5' (2006). Everything on this device — Barracuda, tuxedo, supervis, avahi, mdnsd, vidApp — runs as root on this kernel with no MMU hardening of any modern kind.
impact: Any memory-safety bug in a network-facing component lands on a kernel and libc with none of the last fifteen years of exploit mitigations, so a corruption bug that would be a crash on a modern system is far more likely to be full control here. It also means there is no meaningful privilege boundary to fall back on: the network daemons already run as root. The kernel itself is not directly reachable from the network in an interesting way (no exposed services beyond the TCP/IP stack), which is what keeps this at medium rather than high.
evidence: C:\Users\dev\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\D--PersonalProjects-iot-protocol-tools\000ba43d-52f5-43a6-902d-6c0edfdf3ceb\scratchpad\fw\vmlinux.bin — banner string quoted above. \fw\carved\app2_root\lib\libc-2.5.so — 'GNU C Library stable release version 2.5' and 'glibc 2.5'. \etc\rc.d\init.d\startup launches /supervis and /tuxedo with no user switch; \etc\inittab initdefault runlevel 3 via /etc/rc.d/rcS.
refutation_attempted: I tried to avoid the lazy 'ancient kernel therefore Dirty COW' claim. The honest position: CVE-2016-5195 (Dirty COW) affects 2.6.22 onward and was fixed upstream in October 2016, and this kernel was BUILT in September 2017 — so it is entirely possible the vendor picked up that one patch, and I have no way to tell from a stripped decompressed image without diffing the COW fault path, which I did not do. I therefore do not claim Dirty COW or any other specific kernel CVE. I also checked whether the old kernel is directly network-reachable through some service and it largely is not: no dropbear, sshd, telnetd, inetd, boa, smbd or portmap is started (see the lens summary), so the kernel's exposure is its TCP/IP stack plus whatever the userspace daemons pass down. That materially reduces the finding, and it is why I report this as a mitigation-absence and patch-gap fact rather than an exploitable bug.
fixable_how: Nothing the owner can patch. This is the argument for network isolation as the primary control: an isolated VLAN/SSID for the panel, no inbound from the Internet, no outbound except the specific hosts the panel genuinely needs. Assume that anything which achieves code execution in any panel process has root.

title: avahi 0.6.31 and Apple mDNSResponder both run and answer on UDP/5353
detail: Two independent mDNS implementations ship and are launched. /opt/tuxedo/avahi/sbin/avahi-daemon reports version 0.6.31 (strings '%s 0.6.31 starting up.', '%s 0.6.31 exiting.') — released January 2013, thirteen years old — and /supervis contains the launch string '/opt/tuxedo/avahi/sbin/avahi-daemon -D'. Separately, /mdns/mdnsd is an Apple mDNSResponder '(Engineering Build) (Feb 16 2015 19:37:03)' carrying the version token 'C.487.13536', and /tuxedo contains '/mdns/bonj_client %d &'. Both bind UDP/5353 and parse unauthenticated multicast packets from any host on the local segment. avahi 0.6.31 predates the 2023 family of avahi assertion-failure denial-of-service issues (CVE-2023-38469 through CVE-2023-38473) and has none of those fixes.
impact: Unauthenticated LAN-local packet parsing on the alarm panel, in two separate thirteen- and eleven-year-old C implementations, one of which was not even a release build. The realistic outcome from the known avahi issues is denial of service — a crashed or wedged discovery daemon on the panel — rather than code execution, which is why this is not rated higher. It also means the panel advertises itself on the LAN, which is a discovery convenience for an attacker who is already on the network.
evidence: C:\Users\dev\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\D--PersonalProjects-iot-protocol-tools\000ba43d-52f5-43a6-902d-6c0edfdf3ceb\scratchpad\fw\carved\app2_root\opt\tuxedo\avahi\sbin\avahi-daemon — version strings as quoted; config \opt\tuxedo\avahi\etc\avahi\avahi-daemon.conf. \mdns\mdnsd — '@(#) mDNSResponder (Engineering Build) (Feb 16 2015 19:37:03)', 'C.487.13536'. Launch strings: 'avahi-daemon' and '/opt/tuxedo/avahi/sbin/avahi-daemon -D' in \supervis; '/mdns/bonj_client %d &' in \tuxedo.
refutation_attempted: I went after the one avahi CVE that looked immediately applicable and killed it. CVE-2017-6519 has avahi-daemon answering IPv6 unicast queries from off-link sources, which would turn the panel into a reflector; but /opt/tuxedo/avahi/etc/avahi/avahi-daemon.conf sets 'use-ipv6=no' (with 'use-ipv4=yes'), so that specific issue does not apply to this configuration and I removed it. I also noted the config sets ratelimit-interval-usec=1000000 with ratelimit-burst=1000 and a tight rlimit set (rlimit-nproc=3, rlimit-nofile=768, rlimit-core=0), which blunts naive flooding. Two things I could not resolve: whether mdnsd is actually started at runtime (I only found bonj_client's launch string in /tuxedo, not mdnsd's own — mdnsd may be started by bonj_client or not at all), and the exact upstream mDNSResponder release corresponding to token C.487.13536. detail: Remaining third-party inventory with versions read from the image: zlib 1.2.3 (banner 'deflate 1.2.3 Copyright 1995-2005 Jean-loup Gailly', /usr/lib/libz.so.1.2.3) — 2005, linked by Barracuda, tuxedo and vidApp; libjpeg 6b dated '27-Mar-1998' (/usr/lib/libjpeg.so.62.0.0) — twenty-eight years old, reached via Qt's libqjpeg imageformats plugin which /tuxedo loads explicitly by absolute path, i.e. it decodes IP-camera JPEG frames; expat 2.1.0 (versioned symbol 'expat_2.1.0', /usr/lib/libexpat.so.1.6.0) — 2012, linked only by avahi-daemon, which uses it for local service-definition XML rather than network data; GStreamer core 0.10.28 (string '0.10.28' in /usr/lib/libgstreamer-0.10.so.0.24.1) with a full gst-plugins-base 0.10.19/0.10.24 set — the 0.10 series was abandoned in 2012; Qt 4.8.0 (string '4.8.0' in /home/tuxedo/QT/Build/buildqt480/lib/libQtCore.so.4) — 2011, EOL since 2015, and /tuxedo links QtCore/QtGui/QtNetwork against it. evidence: C:\Users\dev\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\D--PersonalProjects-iot-protocol-tools\000ba43d-52f5-43a6-902d-6c0edfdf3ceb\scratchpad\fw\carved\app2_root\usr\lib\libz.so.1.2.3, \usr\lib\libjpeg.so.62.0.0 ('6b  27-Mar-1998'), \usr\lib\libexpat.so.1.6.0 ('expat_2.1.0'), \usr\lib\libgstreamer-0.10.so.0.24.1 ('0.10.28', 'GStreamer Core Library version %s'), \home\tuxedo\QT\Build\buildqt480\lib\libQtCore.so.4 ('4.8.0'). /tuxedo DT_NEEDED includes the absolute path /home/tuxedo/QT/Build/buildqt480/plugins/imageformats/libqjpeg.so alongside libQtGui.so.4, libQtNetwork.so.4, libz.so.1. avahi-daemon DT_NEEDED: libexpat.so.1.

- No dropbear, no sshd, no telnetd, no boa, no smbd, no inetd binary exists anywhere in the image. /etc/rc.d/init.d/{dropbear,sshd,inetd,boa,smb} all begin with "if [ ! -x <binary> ] then exit 0". /etc/inetd.conf does list telnet -> /usr/sbin/telnetd, but that binary is absent and inetd is never started.
- /etc/rc.d/rc.conf: cfg_services="mount-proc-sys udev hostname depmod modules filesystems" — inetd, portmap, dropbear, sshd, boa, smb, dhcpd are all in all_services but NOT in cfg_services, and /etc/rc.d/rcS only iterates cfg_services. /sbin/portmap exists but is never launched. So no NFS/rpc surface either, despite rpc.mountd/rpc.nfsd/rpc.statd shipping in /usr/sbin.
- /tuxedo has DT_NEEDED libminiupnpc.so.4 but imports NONE of that library's 39 exported symbols — the link is stale. I found no evidence of UPnP-IGD port forwarding (UPNP_AddPortMapping) from any shipped binary, so I do not claim the panel punches its own hole in the router.
- Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160) and CCS injection (CVE-2014-0224) do NOT apply: both were fixed in 1.0.1g and 1.0.1h respectively, and this is exactly 1.0.1h.

FIREWALL PRIORITY FOR THE OWNER (highest first):
1. TCP 80 and 443 on the panel — put the panel on an isolated VLAN/SSID and allow inbound only from the specific hosts that need it. Never port-forward these from the Internet. The HTTPS side gives essentially no confidentiality against anyone who has the firmware (see finding 1), and the HTTP side gives none at all.
2. Outbound HTTPS to tccaps.honeywell.com from the panel — certificate validation is off (finding 2); anyone on-path can impersonate the cloud. Block it if the thermostat cloud feature is unused.
3. UDP 5353 (avahi + mDNSResponder) — LAN-scope only; drop at any router boundary.
4. Outbound RTSP to IP cameras (finding 6) — keep cameras and panel in the same isolated segment; a compromised camera reaches a 2011 live555.

title: Live ECP bus trace switch: /opt/tuxedo/ecpprint/rule (bitmask, re-read instantly via dnotify)
detail: The tuxedo app registers a dnotify watch on the directory /opt/tuxedo/ecpprint and re-reads the file 'rule' whenever anything in that directory is modified. Registration is _Z21regiter_ecp_printrulev @0x59dbf4: it installs _Z24EcpPrintRuleFileModifiediP7siginfoPv (@0x59db7c) via sigaction(12 = SIGUSR2, SA_SIGINFO), opens "/opt/tuxedo/ecpprint" O_RDONLY, then fcntl(fd, F_SETSIG=10, 12) and fcntl(fd, 0x402 = F_NOTIFY, 0x80000002 = DN_MODIFY|DN_MULTISHOT). The handler fopen()s '/opt/tuxedo/ecpprint/rule' mode "r", fscanf("%d") one decimal, then sets two globals from bits: bit0 (value 1) -> g_ecp_rx @0xd977b8, bit1 (value 2) -> g_ecp_tx @0xd97fa0. Shipped file contains "0\n" (all off). The only consumer found is _Z10th_readEcpPv @0x59ce08 (the ECP reader thread, named via prctl(PR_SET_NAME,"Tux_readEcp")): at 0x59ce5c it loads g_ecp_rx and, if non-zero, printf()s the format at 0xc64658 = "ECPRX : %d bytes \n" with the read() return length, on every ECP read. Payload is a per-read byte count, not a frame hex dump. No consumer of g_ecp_tx was found by an exhaustive 4-byte literal scan of the whole file.
impact: Owner gains a zero-restart, on/off trace of ECP receive activity from the panel: one line per ECP read with the byte count, timestamped by whatever is watching the serial console. For protocol work this gives frame boundaries, read cadence, and immediate confirmation that a request actually reached the ECP layer — which is exactly the missing observability in the GetSecurityStatus / RequestPartitionStatus path. Output goes to /tuxedo's stdout, which is inherited from init and therefore lands on /dev/console = ttymxc0 @115200.
evidence: C:/Users/dev/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/D--PersonalProjects-iot-protocol-tools/000ba43d-52f5-43a6-902d-6c0edfdf3ceb/scratchpad/fw/carved/app2_root/opt/tuxedo/ecpprint/rule (2 bytes, "0\n"); tuxedo symbols _Z21regiter_ecp_printrulev @0x59dbf4, _Z24EcpPrintRuleFileModifiediP7siginfoPv @0x59db7c, _Z10th_readEcpPv @0x59ce08; literal pool words at 0x59dbe0-0x59dbf0 resolving to 'r', '/opt/tuxedo/ecpprint/rule' (0xc6484c), '%d', g_ecp_rx (0xd977b8), g_ecp_tx (0xd97fa0); format string 'ECPRX : %d bytes \n' at 0xc64658.
refutation_attempted: I tried to prove this was a dead build-time artifact three ways. (1) Checked whether the rule file is only read once at startup — no: the F_NOTIFY/DN_MULTISHOT + SIGUSR2 registration proves live re-read on every modification. (2) Checked whether g_ecp_rx has any consumer at all — scanned the entire 14.6MB file for the 4-byte literal 0xd977b8 and found exactly two sites, one being the handler and one being th_readEcp, so the flag is genuinely wired. (3) Tried to refute the claim that this yields a useful trace by looking for a fuller dump: I searched all strings for ECPTX/ECP TX/ECP RX variants and found only the single 'ECPRX : %d bytes' format, and found no consumer for g_ecp_tx — so I downgraded the claim from 'full bidirectional frame trace' to 'RX byte-count trace only'. The mechanism survives; the payload is narrower than the symbol names suggest.
fixable_how: Config change, but requires a root shell (serial console, see the U-Boot/runlevel-1 findings) or SD-card write access to the config partition: `echo 1 > /opt/tuxedo/ecpprint/rule` enables RX tracing immediately, `echo 0 >` turns it off. Setting 2 or 3 also sets g_ecp_tx but no code reads it in this build. No firmware patch and no restart needed.

title: U-Boot 2009.01 command shell is present, unlocked, and can netboot the panel over TFTP+NFS
detail: The secondary bootloader image is U-Boot 2009.01 (Jun 17 2015 - 17:52:42) with the full interactive command set: prompt string 'MX35 U-Boot > ', printenv/setenv/saveenv, boot/bootd, nand read, CRC32, tftpboot. I found no password-gated autoboot strings (no 'Enter password', no autoboot keyed-string prompt) anywhere in the image. The default environment also carries a ready-made network boot recipe: bootargs_base='setenv bootargs console=ttymxc0,115200', bootargs_nfs='setenv bootargs ${bootargs} root=/dev/nfs ip=dhcp nfsroot=${serverip}:${nfsroot},v3,tcp', bootcmd_net='run bootargs_base bootargs_nfs; tftpboot ${loadaddr} ${kernel}; bootm', and prg_uboot for reflashing U-Boot itself over TFTP.
