title: The kernel's built-in root= is stale (mtdblock8); the real Root File System is mtd16, and there is a second rootfs slot plus three kernel slots
detail: The decompressed kernel carries a compiled-in command line at file offset 96360: 'noinitrd console=ttymxc0,115200 root=/dev/mtdblock8 rw rootfstype=jffs2 ip=off'. The board's MTD partition-name table in the same image reads, in order: Primary Bootloader, Primary Bootloader Backup, Hardware Parameters Block1..Block7, Secondary BootLoder 1..3, U-Boot Environment variables, Kernel 1, Kernel 2, Kernel 3, Root File System, Second Root File System, PrgCv and BBT. That places 'Root File System' at index 16 and 'Hardware Parameters Block7' at index 8. U-Boot's default environment independently says root=/dev/mtdblock16. Two independent sources agree on 16, and the built-in kernel string points at a hardware-parameter block that could never mount as JFFS2 — so the ATAG command line from U-Boot is what the kernel actually uses (CONFIG_CMDLINE_FORCE is not in effect).
impact: Two things. First, it corrects a working assumption: the rootfs is /dev/mtdblock8 only in a stale compiled-in default; the live root is mtdblock16, and anything scripted against mtdblock8 will read a hardware-parameter block instead. Second, and more useful: the flash layout has three kernel slots and two root filesystem slots. The owner can write an experimental kernel and rootfs into the spare slots and boot them from U-Boot by changing bootargs/bootcmd, keeping the factory image intact as a known-good fallback. That is a real A/B recovery scheme that the product never exposes.
evidence: C:/Users/dev/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/D--PersonalProjects-iot-protocol-tools/000ba43d-52f5-43a6-902d-6c0edfdf3ceb/scratchpad/fw/vmlinux.bin offset 96360 (built-in cmdline) and offsets 3758852-3759296 (partition-name string block: 'Primary Bootloader' .. 'PrgCv and BBT'); C:/.../scratchpad/fw/seconboot.bin offset 156558 'bootargs=noinitrd console=ttymxc0,115200 root=/dev/mtdblock16 rw rootfstype=jffs2'.
refutation_attempted: The weak link is inferring partition indices from the order of .rodata name strings, which is not the same as reading the mtd_partition array. I tried to break it: if the ordering were wrong, U-Boot's independent root=/dev/mtdblock16 would be unlikely to land exactly on the string I counted as index 16 — it does, which is strong corroboration. I also checked whether CONFIG_CMDLINE_FORCE could make the built-in mtdblock8 authoritative; that hypothesis predicts a boot failure (mtdblock8 = a hardware-parameter block, not JFFS2), and the panel demonstrably boots, so it is refuted. I could not statically confirm the exact byte offsets/sizes of each partition, so I have left the index mapping at LIKELY rather than CONFIRMED, and the owner should confirm with `cat /proc/mtd` once they have a shell.
fixable_how: Nothing to enable; this is a correction plus an unused flash layout. Confirm live with `cat /proc/mtd` from a shell, or `nand info` / `printenv` from U-Boot, before writing to any slot.

title: A root shell on the serial console is one bootarg away: sysvinit runlevel 1 respawns /bin/sh -i, and securetty was widened to include ttymxc0
detail: /sbin/init is sysvinit 2.85 (strings 'INIT_VERSION=sysvinit-2.85', 'Switching to runlevel: %c', 'initdefault', 'respawn', 'sysinit'), so the runlevel field in /etc/inittab is honoured. /etc/inittab sets 'id:3:initdefault:' and contains 'l1:1:respawn:/bin/sh -i' — an unauthenticated root shell in runlevel 1 — plus a commented-out 'co:2345:respawn:/bin/sh -i' that would have given the same shell in the normal runlevel. /bin/sh is a symlink to bash. Separately, /etc/securetty has been modified from its shipped original (/etc/securetty.orig is still present for comparison) specifically to add 'console', 'ttymxc0', 'ttymxc1', 'ttymxc/0', 'ttymxc/1' — the vendor deliberately made the i.MX35 serial ports valid login terminals. /sbin/getty and /sbin/agetty exist and /bin/login is a symlink to tinylogin. Console is already ttymxc0,115200 per the kernel cmdline.
impact: The owner can get an interactive root prompt on the panel with a serial cable and no soldering of a debug header beyond the existing ttymxc0 pins, without flashing anything. That unlocks every other finding in this report — the ECP trace switch, WebConfig edits, reading SupervisionLog.txt, mq_read, /proc inspection.
evidence: /etc/inittab and /etc/securetty vs /etc/securetty.orig under C:/Users/dev/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/D--PersonalProjects-iot-protocol-tools/000ba43d-52f5-43a6-902d-6c0edfdf3ceb/scratchpad/fw/carved/app2_root/etc/; /sbin/init strings at offsets 22196 '/etc/inittab', 23120 'INIT_VERSION=sysvinit-2.85', 22860 'Switching to runlevel: %c', 24048 'respawn'; /bin/sh -> bash, /bin/login -> tinylogin, /sbin/getty -> ../bin/tinylogin; kernel cmdline console=ttymxc0,115200.
refutation_attempted: I attacked this from two sides. (1) Is the runlevel field actually honoured? If init were BusyBox, the runlevel column is ignored and all respawn entries run — which would mean the shell is already live on the console. I checked and it is real sysvinit 2.85, so the shell is gated on runlevel 1 and is NOT running in the default runlevel 3. (2) Would passing '1' work? sysvinit maps the kernel arg 'single'/'-s' to runlevel S, and this inittab has no S entry and no sulogin line, so 'single' alone would likely drop to nothing useful; the numeric '1' maps to the l1 entry. I also noted /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow are absent from the image entirely, which means the login/getty path probably cannot authenticate anyone — another reason the runlevel-1 respawn shell (which bypasses login) is the right route rather than adding a getty. I could not test this on hardware, hence LIKELY. Note also that /etc/rc.d/rcS runs as sysinit regardless of runlevel, so /tuxedo and the web server will still start.
fixable_how: Config change at boot, no firmware patch: stop U-Boot autoboot, `setenv bootargs 'noinitrd console=ttymxc0,115200 root=/dev/mtdblock16 rw rootfstype=jffs2 ip=off 1'` then `boot` (do not `saveenv` unless you want it permanent). Use the numeric 1, not 'single'. Once in, `telinit 3` returns to the normal runlevel.

title: Dropbear, sshd, telnetd, inetd and syslogd have init scripts but the binaries are absent — SSH cannot be enabled without adding files
detail: /etc/rc.d/init.d/ ships working start/stop scripts for dropbear, sshd, inetd, syslog, boa, dhcpd, portmap and smb, and /etc/inetd.conf has the telnet line UNCOMMENTED ('telnet stream tcp nowait root /usr/sbin/telnetd telnetd', with the header comment 'seh: from netkit-base-0.17 but with shell enable for auto-test'). But /etc/rc.d/rc.conf reduces the runlist to cfg_services="mount-proc-sys udev hostname depmod modules filesystems" — dropbear, sshd, inetd, syslog and boa are all excluded. More decisively, I enumerated every file in /bin, /sbin, /usr/bin, /usr/sbin and /usr/local/sbin: there is no dropbear, no dropbearkey, no sshd, no ssh-keygen, no telnetd, no inetd, no boa, no syslogd and no klogd anywhere in the image. Each init script also guards itself with `if [ ! -x /usr/sbin/<daemon> ]; then exit 0; fi`, so even adding them to cfg_services is a no-op.
impact: This is a negative result worth having: it closes off the most obvious 'just turn on SSH' avenue and saves the owner from editing rc.conf and rebooting to no effect. Network shell access on this box means cross-compiling and installing a static dropbear (or a BusyBox with telnetd) yourself, which is a much bigger job than flipping a config line — so serial console is the correct first move, not SSH. It also means there is no syslog daemon: nothing is collecting /dev/log, and kernel/app messages exist only on the serial console and in the app's own files.
evidence: C:/Users/dev/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/D--PersonalProjects-iot-protocol-tools/000ba43d-52f5-43a6-902d-6c0edfdf3ceb/scratchpad/fw/carved/app2_root/etc/rc.d/rc.conf (cfg_services line), /etc/rc.d/init.d/{dropbear,sshd,inetd,syslog,boa}, /etc/inetd.conf (telnet line enabled); full directory listings of /bin, /sbin, /usr/bin, /usr/sbin, /usr/local/sbin showing none of dropbear/sshd/telnetd/inetd/boa/syslogd/klogd present.

I also checked whether the daemons might live on a second partition mounted at runtime; /etc/fstab and the startup script mount only /tmp, /var (tmpfs), /dev/mq and optionally SD, nothing that would supply /usr/sbin. The finding survives.

If network shell is wanted: cross-compile a static dropbear for ARMv6 EABI, place it at /usr/sbin/dropbear, add 'dropbear' to cfg_services in /etc/rc.d/rc.conf. Note the panel is a security device on a home LAN — serial-only access is the safer choice, and a listening SSH daemon on it is a new attack surface.

title: Event callback / webhook registration (Administration/AddIPURL) — the panel can push events to a URL you choose instead of being polled
detail: Barracuda implements an Administration/AddIPURL family with handler symbols setAddIPURL, getAddIPURL, setUpdateIPURL, getUpdateIPURL, setViewIPURL, getViewIPURL in .symtab, plus error strings 'Invalid parameters for AddIPURL', 'Invalid parameters for UpdateIPURL', 'Invalid parameters for ViewIPURL'. The compiled-in HTML form for it collects: Device MAC (registered MAC address), Device IP, Device Port, 'URL address ... URL to be updated on events', and 'Query String Name ... Query String name in which events to be updated'. The example URL form is /system_http_api/API_REV01/Administration/AddIPURL?mac=<MAC ID>&IP=<Device IP>&url=<Call back server link>&operation=set. The web UI has hyperlinks for all three (ancaddipurl/ancupdateipurl/ancviewipurl) but they are shipped with style="display:none", and the UpdateIPURL doc block is HTML-commented out.
impact: If it works as documented, the panel becomes push rather than pull: register an HTTP endpoint on the owner's own server and the panel notifies it on events, instead of the owner polling GetSecurityStatus/GetEvent on a timer. That removes the polling load, removes the latency floor, and sidesteps a good deal of the session/timeout churn. For a home-automation integration this is the single highest-leverage unexposed feature found.

title: Web-server feature flags and session timeout live in a plain-text file: /root/Settings/WebConfig.conf
detail: Barracuda reads /root/Settings/WebConfig.conf line by line (fgets with a 100-byte buffer, split on ':', atoi) through a set of named getters, one per key. The shipped file is: No_Of_Users:10, Session_Timer:10, User_Code:01, Display_Text:01, Allow_Security:01, Allow_Multimedia:01, Allow_HomeAutomation:01, Home_Automation_TopMenu:00, Allow_Zwave_Install:00, Login_Enabled:01, VoiceEnabled:00, Allow_VideoRecording:01, Allow_API:01. Confirmed key-to-getter mapping by resolving each key string's address and finding its referencing function: Session_Timer -> getMaxSessionTimeOut @0x7177c and _Z18getMaxSessionTimerv; Login_Enabled -> getLoginEnabled; Allow_API -> allowSystemAPIFromConfig; No_Of_Users -> getNoOfUsersFromConfig; Allow_Security -> allowSecurityFromConfig; Display_Text -> GetDisplayTextFromConfig; plus allowMultimediaFromConfig, allowHomeAutomationFromConfig, allowVideoRecordingFromConfig, getHomeAutomationTopMenuFromConfig, userCodeRequiredFromConfig, getNoOfConnectedUsers, getTotalItemsInWebConfig, getFromWebConfig. Disassembly of getMaxSessionTimeOut @0x7177c shows the hardcoded fallback is 0x14 = 20 when the file or key is missing; the shipped value is 10. There is also a key 'Connected_No_Of_Users' recognised by the code but not present in the shipped file.
impact: The web session timeout that forces a long-running integration to re-authenticate is a single number in a text file, as is the concurrent-user cap and each feature area's on/off state. Raising Session_Timer materially reduces re-login churn for any client that polls; raising No_Of_Users lets more clients connect at once. This is the cheapest tuning surface on the device and it needs no code change at all.

refutation_attempted: I checked that these are not compile-time constants with the file as decoration: the disassembly of getMaxSessionTimeOut shows a real fopen/fgets/strstr/atoi loop with a fallback constant, so the file wins when present. I could not determine the unit of Session_Timer (minutes is the obvious reading given the value 10 and a default of 20, but I found no multiply-by-60 in the getter itself, so the conversion happens in the caller and I have not verified it) — I have deliberately not claimed 'minutes' as fact. I also verified /root is on the JFFS2 rootfs mounted rw per bootargs, so the file is genuinely editable and persistent, not on a tmpfs that resets.
fixable_how: Config change, needs a root shell (or an SD-card path that can write /root). Edit /root/Settings/WebConfig.conf, e.g. Session_Timer:60, and restart Barracuda (supervis relaunches it: `killall Barracuda` and it comes back, per E_SUPVTRD_BARRACUDA_RESTART). Keep a copy of the original file first. Do not set Login_Enabled:00 — that is the web login gate.

title: The web server's listening port is configurable via Tuxedo.json (BARRACUDA -> PORT_NUMBER), default 6280
detail: getBarracudaPort @0x314b8 in Barracuda does not read WebConfig.conf despite the PORT_NUMBER string sitting in that key cluster. It opens /opt/tuxedo/configuration/Tuxedo.json (with /opt/tuxedo/configuration/Tuxedo_sec.json as the shadow/backup, compared and resynced first), parses it as JSON, walks to the object member 'BARRACUDA' (string at 0x8f55c), reads the member 'PORT_NUMBER' (string at 0x90104) and converts it to an integer. On any failure — file missing, JSON parse failure, wrong node types, key absent — it returns the hardcoded literal 0x1888 = 6280. Separately the PFTable holds TUX_HTTP_EXT_PORT and TUX_HTTPS_EXT_PORT, which are external/mapped port values, not the listener.
impact: The owner can move the panel's web listener without touching code — useful for putting it behind a reverse proxy, avoiding a port clash, or simply knowing which port to probe when the UI appears unreachable. Equally important as a diagnostic fact: if Tuxedo.json is damaged or its BARRACUDA node is missing, the server silently falls back to 6280 rather than failing loudly, which looks exactly like 'the web interface died'.
evidence: Barracuda getBarracudaPort @0x314b8, disassembled: literal pool resolves to '/opt/tuxedo/configuration/Tuxedo.json' (0x8f508), '/opt/tuxedo/configuration/Tuxedo_sec.json' (0x8f530), 'BARRACUDA' (0x8f55c), 'PORT_NUMBER' (0x90104), and the fallback constant 0x1888 loaded at 0x314fc / 0x315d8 / 0x315e4. 'BARRACUDA' also appears as a plain .rodata string at offset 554332 alongside 'LocalLogin' and 'HTTPS'.
refutation_attempted: My first reading was wrong and I corrected it: because 'PORT_NUMBER' sits immediately among the WebConfig.conf keys in .rodata I initially assumed it was a WebConfig key. Disassembling the getter refuted that — the file opened is Tuxedo.json, not WebConfig.conf. I then checked whether 0x1888 might be something other than a port (a buffer size, a timeout); it is the value returned on every error path of a function named getBarracudaPort and is returned in r0 as the function result, so it is the default port. I have not verified which port the device actually listens on in practice, since Tuxedo.json is generated at runtime and is not present in the firmware image.
fixable_how: Config change: edit the BARRACUDA.PORT_NUMBER member of /opt/tuxedo/configuration/Tuxedo.json (and keep Tuxedo_sec.json consistent — the code compares and resyncs them) and restart Barracuda. Verify the live value first with `netstat -lnt` from a shell rather than assuming 6280.

title: supervis already keeps a persistent crash and restart log, and the touchscreen has a one-button 'copy all config to SD card' that extracts it without a shell
detail: /supervis is launched by /etc/rc.d/init.d/startup and is the process watchdog: it opens /dev/watchdog and kicks it, monitors tuxedo, Barracuda, TotalConnect, vidApp, audioapp, VoiceRecog, wpa_supplicant, dhclient and others by scanning /proc/<pid>/stat, counts open pipes via `ls -l /proc/%d/fd | grep "pipe" | wc -l`, reads memory usage from /proc/%d/statm, relaunches dead processes ('/tuxedo &', '/opt/webserver/Barracuda &', '/vidrec/vidApp &', '/audioapp &', '/TotalConnect &'), and restarts the whole system when relaunch limits are exceeded. It timestamps and appends everything to /opt/tuxedo/configuration/SupervisionLog.txt using the format '%a %b %d %Y, %H:%M:%S' + '%s - %s'. Recorded event names include E_SUPVTRD_TUXEDO_RECV_SIGSEGV, E_SUPVTRD_TUXEDO_RECV_SIGABRT, E_SUPVTRD_TUXEDO_MSGQ_OVERFLOW, E_SUPVTRD_BARRACUDA_RECV_SIGSEGV/SIGABRT/MSGQ_OVERFLOW, E_SUPVTRD_BARRACUDA_RESTART-%d, E_SUPVTRD_POWER_MANAGEMENT_EVENTS, E_SUPVTRD_WIFIDRVR_ERROR, MAX_OPEN_PIPES ERROR, BarracudaMemoryusageExceeded, VidappMemoryusageExceeded, 'SYSTEM RESTART DUE TO MAX RECOVERY/RELAUNCH limit exeeded'. Separately, the touchscreen's Advanced Setup screen has a slot CAdvSetup::sltHandleConfSDClicked() whose body issues `cp -rf /opt/tuxedo/configuration /mnt/sd/` — copying the entire configuration directory, SupervisionLog.txt included, to an inserted SD card. The same directory also holds AuiEventLogFile.txt (the AUI event log, written by AddAUIEvent and rolled over by AuiEventFileRollOver), HaActionLog.txt, panelinfo.txt, CRCdata.json, userdetails.json and the network/wifi configs.
impact: The panel has been recording its own crash, memory-exhaustion and restart history all along, and there is a supported, no-shell, no-soldering way to get it off the device: insert an SD card and press the Config-to-SD button in Advanced Setup. For anyone diagnosing intermittent web-server death, panel reboots, or the status-cache problem, that log is the first thing to read, and it costs nothing to obtain.

The startup script has '#/supervis &' commented near the top, which looks like it is disabled — but further down the same file has an uncommented '/supervis &' followed by 'sleep 2' before '/tuxedo &'. title: Barracuda already collects fine-grained per-feature usage counters into /opt/tuxedo/Log/v5WebData.json and never surfaces them
detail: Barracuda maintains two counter structures, 'WebApiData' and 'WebAccessData', and serialises them to /opt/tuxedo/Log/v5WebData.json (creating the parent directory, with the error string 'error in creating PARENT FILE DIR'). The counter names are compiled in as a printf block headed '---V5WebApiData Structure Values---' and '---V5WebData Structure Values---' and include, on the API side: NOOF_API_SECURITY_DISARM, NOOF_API_SECURITY_ARM, NOOF_API_SECURITY_ZONE_OPERATION, NOOF_API_AUT_LIGHT_ON/OFF, NOOF_API_AUTOMATION_DOOR_LOCK/UNLOCK, thermostat mode and setpoint changes, GDO open/close, water valve open/close, NOOF_API_SCENE_EXE_CNT, NOOF_API_LOCAL_USAGE_CNT, NOOF_API_REMOTE_USAGE_CNT, API_ACCESSED_DEVICE_TYPE_CNT; and on the web-UI side per-page access counts: NOOF_WEB_SECURITY_PAGE_ACCESS, NOOF_WEB_EVENTVIEW_PAGE_ACCESS, NOOF_WEB_CONSOLE_PAGE_ACCESS, NOOF_WEB_MOBILE_CONSOLE_PAGE_ACCESS, NOOF_WEB_CAMERA_SETUP_PAGE_ACCESS, NOOF_WEB_LOCAL_ACCESS_CNT, NOOF_WEB_REMOTE_ACCESS_CNT, NOOF_WEB_USER, and arm/disarm counts. Notably NOOF_API_SECURITY_ZONE_OPERATION exists as a counter even though no zone command code is exposed in the web app.
impact: A ready-made audit trail of who used what, split local vs remote and API vs web UI, is already being written to disk. For an owner it answers 'is anything still talking to this panel', 'did that arm come from the web or the API', and 'is my integration actually hitting the endpoints I think it is' — without adding any instrumentation. It is also a small independent hint that a zone operation path exists somewhere in the API surface, which is worth noting against the documented negative that no zone command code exists in the web app.
evidence: Barracuda .rodata: '/opt/tuxedo/Log' at offset 557176, 'error in creating PARENT FILE DIR' at 557192, 'WebAccessData' at 557228, 'WebApiData' at 557244, '/opt/tuxedo/Log/v5WebData.json' at 557256 ; the counter-name printf block spanning offsets 555140-557176 including 'NOOF_API_SECURITY_ZONE_OPERATION--->%d,%d' at 555316.
refutation_attempted: I tried to dismiss these as debug printf format strings that are never reached. Against that: the same names sit adjacent to the JSON output path and the two structure names, and the code creates the parent directory, which is behaviour you only write for a file you intend to produce. What I could NOT do is confirm the write actually happens on this build — I did not trace a caller chain from a request handler down to the serialiser, and /opt/tuxedo/Log is empty in the firmware image (as expected for a runtime directory, but it is not proof). The NOOF_API_SECURITY_ZONE_OPERATION counter is a hint about zone support, not evidence of a reachable zone command, and I am explicitly not claiming it overturns the documented negative — a counter name can outlive the feature it counted.
fixable_how: Already enabled if it works. Check for /opt/tuxedo/Log/v5WebData.json from a shell. Note this file is under /opt/tuxedo/Log, not /opt/tuxedo/configuration, so the Advanced Setup Config-to-SD button does NOT pick it up — you need shell access or to copy it manually.

title: Verbose kernel logging and crash core dumps are pre-written into the startup script, commented out
detail: /etc/rc.d/init.d/startup contains three diagnostic lines the vendor left in place but disabled: '#echo 8 > /proc/sys/kernel/printk' (raise the console log level so all kernel messages reach ttymxc0), '#ulimit -c unlimited' and '#echo "/mnt/sd/coredump" > /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern' (write process core dumps to the SD card), and '#export MALLOC_CHECK_=1' (glibc heap consistency checking). The same file actively sets kernel.panic=5, kernel.panic_on_oops=1 and kernel.hung_task_panic=1 — so the panel currently reboots on an oops or a hung task rather than leaving evidence. /etc/rc.d/rcS carries the same commented printk line. Separately, the tuxedo app names every thread with prctl(PR_SET_NAME) — for example th_readEcp registers as 'Tux_readEcp' — so /proc/<pid>/task/*/comm gives readable thread names once you have a shell.
impact: Turning these on converts an opaque reboot into a diagnosable event: full kernel messages on the console, and a core file on the SD card for any tuxedo or Barracuda crash that supervis currently just logs and restarts past. Combined with SupervisionLog.txt (which tells you a SIGSEGV happened) a core dump tells you where. The prctl thread names make `top -H` and /proc walking immediately legible instead of a wall of identical process names.
evidence: C:/Users/dev/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/D--PersonalProjects-iot-protocol-tools/000ba43d-52f5-43a6-902d-6c0edfdf3ceb/scratchpad/fw/carved/app2_root/etc/rc.d/init.d/startup (commented printk / ulimit -c / core_pattern / MALLOC_CHECK_ lines, and the active sysctl panic settings) ; /etc/rc.d/rcS (same commented printk line) ; tuxedo _Z10th_readEcpPv @0x59ce08 calling prctl with r0=#0xf (PR_SET_NAME) and the string 'Tux_readEcp' at 0xc6492c.
refutation_attempted: I checked whether these would be ineffective even if uncommented. printk level 8 is standard and the console is already ttymxc0, so that one is sound. The core_pattern line depends on an SD card being mounted at /mnt/sd at the time of the crash — /mnt/sd exists as a mount point and the SD insert/remove scripts are in /opt/tuxedo/scripts, but if no card is present the dump is simply lost, so this is conditional rather than guaranteed. I also confirmed kernel.panic_on_oops=1 and kernel.hung_task_panic=1 are actively set (not commented), which is what makes the panel reboot instead of preserving state — worth knowing before chasing an intermittent fault. I verified the prctl claim by reading the argument register (r0 = 0xf = PR_SET_NAME) rather than assuming from the string alone.
fixable_how: Config change requiring a root shell and a writable rootfs (it is mounted rw). Uncomment the lines in /etc/rc.d/init.d/startup, or apply them live without editing anything: `echo 8 > /proc/sys/kernel/printk` and `echo /mnt/sd/coredump > /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern` with a card inserted. Consider also relaxing kernel.hung_task_panic while investigating, so a stall leaves a console trace instead of an immediate reboot.

title: Barracuda's SimpleDebugger HTTP trace console is half-present: the browser-side controls ship in the web app, but the server-side handlers were removed
detail: The web app ships Barracuda's SimpleDebugger EventHandler stubs. autogen/SimpleDbgServer2ClientIntf.txt declares a server-to-client method asynchOnInitSetStatus(traceButtonState, tracePriorityLevel, requestEnabled, requestHeadersEnabled, responseHeadersEnabled, http11StateEnabled), and autogen/SimpleDbgClient2ServerIntf.js implements client-to-server calls setTraceButtonState, setTraceLevel, setRequest, setRequestHeaders, setResponseHeaders, setHttp11State and numberOfClients. The full Barracuda HttpTrace API is linked into the binary (HttpTrace_constructor, setBufSize, setFLushCallback, setPrio, setRequest, setRequestHeaders, setResponseHeaders, setResponseBody, setHttp11State, setReqBufOverflow, getTraceCmds, write, printf, vprintf, flush), and SimpleDebugger_send2Browser / _newClientCon / _clientConTerminated / _vprintf all exist. HOWEVER: a byte search of the Barracuda ELF for the literal method-name strings 'setTrace', 'setRequest', 'setHttp11', 'numberOfClients', 'Client2ServerIntf' and even 'Trace' returns zero hits in the code/data image — only the server-to-client names 'statusMessageText' (offset 538488), 'noOfClient' (538964) and 'SimpleDbgServer2ClientIntf' (538936) are present. A BL-scan of .text found no external caller of HttpTrace_setBufSize or HttpTrace_setFLushCallback, meaning HttpTrace is never constructed and every HttpTrace_write in createServer() is inert. The vendor kept the SimpleDebugger transport and repurposed it purely as the event push channel: bprintf @0x1e0f4 -> SimpleDebugger_vprintf -> send2Browser, called 117 times from gettuxedoIPCCommFunc (the thread draining the message queue from /tuxedo).
impact: This is a negative result that saves real time. The obvious lead — 'there is a debug console in the firmware, wire up the shipped JS and get live HTTP request/response header tracing in the browser' — does not work on this build. The /SimpleDebugger.interface endpoint is real and is exactly the channel script/eventHandler.js already uses for panel events, but it accepts no trace-control calls. What is genuinely usable from it is the event stream itself, including an unused server-to-client method partList(text) that the shipped UI leaves as an empty stub.

refutation_attempted: I assumed the opposite first and tried to prove the trace controls WERE live. I searched the strings dump, then re-searched the raw ELF bytes directly in case the strings extractor had missed short or non-ASCII-adjacent literals — zero hits, while the server-to-client names in the same dispatch family are all present, which is the decisive asymmetry. I then checked whether HttpTrace might be initialised from somewhere I had not looked by BL-scanning all of .text for calls to HttpTrace_setBufSize and HttpTrace_setFLushCallback (the only two functions that call HttpTrace_constructor) and found no external callers. Finally I confirmed the interface is not simply dead by tracing bprintf's 117 call sites in gettuxedoIPCCommFunc, which shows the channel is alive and carrying app events. The negative survives.
fixable_how: Needs a firmware patch, so not worth pursuing. Do not spend time wiring up the shipped SimpleDbgClient2ServerIntf.js. Instead, use /SimpleDebugger.interface as the event push channel it actually is — the same one script/eventHandler.js uses — and consider implementing the unused partList(text) callback in your own client to see whether the server ever pushes a partition list on it.
